88883.q: What do you call a heap of lots and lots of tiny soap bubbles?
88883.e: Foam is made of countless tiny bubbles stuck together. You see it in the bath, for example.
88883.m: Foam is made of lots of small soap bubbles.

88884.q: What happens if soapy water gets in your eyes?
88884.e: Soap irritates the sensitive eyes. It is best to rinse them with clear water.
88884.m: Soapy water stings in your eyes.

88885.q: Roughly how many times a minute does an adult breathe at rest?
88885.e: An adult at rest breathes about 12 to 18 times a minute. When working hard, it is more.
88885.m: An adult at rest breathes about 15 times a minute.

88886.q: Do children breathe faster or slower than adults?
88886.e: Children have smaller lungs. That is why they breathe more times a minute than adults.

88887.e: When you run, your muscles work hard and need more oxygen. That is why you breathe faster and deeper.
88887.m: You breathe faster when you work hard.

88888.q: Roughly how much air does an adult breathe in with one calm breath?
88888.e: With one calm breath, about half a litre of air flows into the lungs. With a deep breath it is much more.
88888.m: A calm breath is about half a litre of air.

88889.q: Do we breathe when we are asleep?
88889.e: The brain controls breathing automatically. That is why we also breathe in our sleep without thinking about it.
88889.m: We breathe all by ourselves when we sleep.

88890.q: What does one whole breath consist of?
88890.e: A breath starts with breathing in and ends with breathing out. Then the next one begins.
88890.m: A breath consists of breathing in and breathing out.

88891.q: Roughly how many breaths does an adult take in a day?
88891.e: Because we breathe day and night without a break, we take over 20,000 breaths every day.
88891.m: A person breathes over 20,000 times every day.

88892.e: When you sigh, you breathe in especially deeply and breathe out so it can be heard. It often happens all by itself.
88892.m: A sigh is an especially deep breath.

88893.q: Why do pot plants sometimes die if you water them far too much?
88893.e: Roots also need oxygen from tiny air spaces in the soil. If the soil is always under water, they don't get this air.
88893.m: Plant roots also need air in the soil.

88894.e: Green plants and algae make oxygen using sunlight. They release it into the air and water.

88895.q: What bubbles in an aquarium so that the fish have enough oxygen?
88895.e: An air pump blows small bubbles into the water. This puts more oxygen into the water.
88895.m: An air pump brings oxygen into the aquarium.

88896.q: Why do fish in a warm pond sometimes gulp for air at the surface?
a: The water is short of oxygen
88896.e: Warm water can hold less oxygen than cold water. When oxygen is short, fish gulp for air at the top.

88897.q: What does a small device clipped onto your finger in hospital measure?
88897.e: The device shines light through the finger. That way it can tell how much oxygen the blood is carrying.
88897.m: A finger clip measures the oxygen in the blood.

88898.q: Which letter is used for oxygen in chemistry?
88898.e: The symbol O comes from the Latin name “oxygenium”. This is how oxygen is written in chemistry.

88899.q: What happens to a cut apple that is left in the air for a long time?
88899.e: Substances in the apple react with the oxygen in the air. This makes the cut surface turn brown.
88899.m: A cut apple turns brown in the air.

88900.q: What colour is the oxygen in the air?
88900.e: Oxygen is a gas with no colour and no smell. That is why we cannot see it.

88901.q: How much carbon dioxide does the air contain?
88901.e: Only a tiny part of the air is carbon dioxide, less than one thousandth. Even so, it matters for plants and for the climate.
88901.m: The air contains only very little carbon dioxide.

88902.q: Roughly how much of the air is oxygen?
88902.e: Oxygen makes up about 21 out of 100 parts of the air. That is roughly a fifth.
88902.m: About a fifth of the air is oxygen.

88903.q: How can you tell outdoors that the air is moving?
88903.e: We call moving air wind. We feel it on our skin and see the leaves move.
88903.m: We feel moving air as wind.

88904.q: What makes the air in a stuffy room fresh again?
88904.e: When you air a room, fresh air flows in from outside. The stale air goes out.
88904.m: Airing a room brings in fresh air.

88905.q: What pollutes the air we breathe in towns and cities?
88905.e: Cars, heating systems and factories give off exhaust fumes into the air. These can irritate the airways.
88905.m: Exhaust fumes pollute the air we breathe.

88906.q: Is there still oxygen in the air we breathe out?
88906.e: Breathed-out air still contains about 16 out of 100 parts oxygen. That is why rescue breaths can help another person.
88906.m: Even breathed-out air still contains oxygen.

88907.q: Where is the air usually cleaner?
88907.e: No cars drive in the woods and the trees filter dust out of the air. That is why the air there is usually cleaner.
88907.m: The air in the woods is usually clean.

88908.q: What does cigarette smoke do to the lungs?
88908.e: Smoke contains many poisonous substances. They settle in the lungs and can make them ill.

88909.q: In winter the air indoors is often very dry. Which device helps with this?
88909.e: A humidifier releases water into the air as a fine mist or steam. This helps against very dry air from the heating.
88909.m: A humidifier makes dry air moister.

88910.q: Why is ice on the pavement dangerous?
88910.e: On smooth ice your shoes hardly grip. You can easily slip and fall over.
88910.m: Ice on the pavement is very slippery.

88911.q: Where does a lake freeze first in winter?
a: In the middle of the water
Under the sand on the shore
88911.e: The cold air cools the water from above. That is why the layer of ice forms first on top of the lake.
88911.m: A lake freezes from the top.

88912.q: Why can fish survive under a frozen lake?
a: The water under the ice stays liquid
88912.e: Under the ice, the water stays liquid and a little warmer. There the fish can go on living.
88912.m: Under the ice, the water stays liquid.

88913.q: What are the white specks you often see in an ice cube?
88913.e: There is some air dissolved in water. When it freezes, this air gets trapped in the ice as tiny bubbles.
88913.m: White specks in ice are air bubbles.

88914.q: What do you need an ice scraper for in winter?
a: To remove ice from the car window
88914.e: After cold nights the car window is often covered in ice. You scrape it off with the ice scraper so you can see properly again.
88914.m: You clear ice off the car window with an ice scraper.

88915.q: How do you turn an open space into a natural ice rink in winter?
a: You spray water on it when it is freezing
88915.e: When it is freezing, you spray water onto the space in several thin layers. Each layer freezes until a smooth ice surface forms.
88915.m: For a natural ice rink, you spray water on in frosty weather.

88916.q: What does an ice pack do in a picnic bag?
88916.e: An ice pack is frozen in the freezer. In the bag it takes in heat and so keeps the food cool for longer.
88916.m: An ice pack keeps food cool.

88917.q: How does the ice of an artificial ice rink stay frozen even when it is above zero?
a: Cooling pipes lie under the ice
Lots of salt is scattered on it
88917.e: Under the surface of an artificial ice rink run pipes with a very cold liquid. They cool the ice from below.
88917.m: Cooling pipes keep the ice of an artificial rink frozen.

88918.q: What do you often hear when you put ice cubes into a warm drink?
88918.e: The outside of the ice cube suddenly gets warm while the inside stays cold. This creates fine cracks that crackle.
88918.m: Ice cubes crack in warm drinks.

88919.q: Why do you put ice cubes in a drink?
88919.e: The ice cubes take heat out of the drink. This makes the drink cooler.

88920.q: What colour is pure water in a glass?
88920.e: Pure water in a glass is colourless and see-through. You can look through it.

88921.q: How much of our body is made of water?
88921.e: An adult's body is more than half water. That is why we have to drink every day.
88921.m: Our body is more than half water.

88922.q: What happens when you pour water into a different bowl?
a: It takes the shape of the bowl
88922.e: Water is liquid and has no fixed shape. It fits any container.
88922.m: Water takes the shape of its container.

88923.q: What usually comes out of the tap when you turn it to the side marked red?
88923.e: On many mixer taps, red stands for hot and blue for cold water. That way you know which way to turn.
88923.m: Red on a tap stands for hot water.

88924.q: What happens to a dry sponge when you put it in water?
88924.e: A sponge has lots of small holes. The water gets in and fills them, so the sponge gets heavy and wet.

88925.q: About how much should schoolchildren drink each day?
88925.e: The Swiss Society for Nutrition recommends about one litre a day for children aged 6 to 12, ideally water or unsweetened tea. In hot weather and during sport you need more.
88925.m: Schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day.

88926.q: In which unit do you measure water in a measuring jug?
88926.e: A measuring jug shows litres, decilitres or millilitres. You use it to measure how much liquid is in it.
88926.m: In a measuring jug you measure water in litres.

88927.q: What does a sign saying “Not drinking water” on a fountain mean?
a: You should not drink from it
88927.e: Not all fountain water is checked and clean enough to drink. The sign warns you not to drink it.
88927.m: If it says “Not drinking water”, do not drink from the fountain.

88928.q: What state is water in at 20 degrees Celsius?
88928.e: At room temperature, water is neither frozen nor boiling. It is liquid.
88928.m: At room temperature, water is liquid.

88929.q: What can hot steam cause on the skin?
88929.e: Hot steam gives off a lot of heat to the skin. That can cause painful scalds.
88929.m: Hot steam can scald the skin.

88930.q: Where does warm steam from a pan go?
88930.e: Warm steam is lighter than the cooler air around it. That is why it rises.

88931.q: What do you use a steam iron for?
a: To get creases out of clothes
88931.e: The hot steam makes the fabric soft. Then you can smooth out the creases with the iron.

88932.q: How can you cook vegetables gently in the kitchen?
88932.e: When steaming, the vegetables sit above boiling water. The hot steam cooks them without them lying in the water.
88932.m: You can cook vegetables gently over steam.

88933.q: What whistles in the kitchen when the water in it boils?
88933.e: The steam flows through a small opening in the spout. This makes a loud whistling sound.
88933.m: A whistling kettle whistles when steam comes out.

88934.q: What forms in the sauna when you pour water onto the hot stones?
88934.e: On the very hot stones, the water turns into steam at once. This makes the air damp and it feels hotter.
88934.m: In the sauna, water on hot stones turns into steam.

88935.q: Why does the lid on a pan of boiling water sometimes rattle?
88935.e: Boiling water makes a lot of steam. It pushes against the lid from below and lifts it briefly again and again.
88935.m: Steam can lift a pan lid.

88936.q: What does a steam cleaner clean with?
88936.e: A steam cleaner heats water and blows the hot steam onto floors or tiles. The steam loosens the dirt.
88936.m: A steam cleaner cleans with hot steam.

88937.q: What does a coffee machine use to froth the milk?
88937.e: Hot steam streams into the milk from a thin tube. It warms the milk and blows air into it, which makes froth.

88938.q: What melts easily in a warm hand?
88938.e: Chocolate gets soft and runny even from the warmth of your hand. Stones, wood and glass, on the other hand, do not melt.
88938.m: Chocolate melts even in a warm hand.

88939.q: What do you melt in the caquelon for a fondue?
88939.e: For a cheese fondue, grated cheese is warmed in the caquelon until it is runny. Then you dip bread into it.
88939.m: For a fondue, you melt cheese.

88940.q: Why do you have to eat an ice cream quickly in summer?
88940.e: Ice cream is frozen. In the summer heat it quickly gets soft and drips.
88940.m: In summer an ice cream melts quickly.

88941.q: What quickly turns liquid in a hot frying pan?
88941.e: Butter is solid in the fridge. In the hot pan it quickly melts into a yellow liquid.
88941.m: Butter melts in a hot pan.

88942.q: What is often left when a snowman has melted in spring?
a: A puddle and the carrot nose
88942.e: The snow turns into water and forms a puddle. Carrots, stones or coal do not melt and are left lying there.
88942.m: A melted snowman leaves a puddle.

88943.q: What melts in a hot glue gun?
88943.e: In the hot glue gun, a plastic stick is heated. It melts and comes out at the front as liquid glue.
88943.m: In a hot glue gun, a glue stick melts.

88944.q: What is the Swiss dish called where cheese is melted by a heater and scraped off?
88944.e: For raclette, half a wheel of cheese or cheese in little pans is heated. The melted cheese is poured over potatoes.

88945.q: What happens to marshmallows that you toast over the fire?
88945.e: The heat makes the sugar in the marshmallow melt. That is why it gets soft and sticky inside.
88945.m: Over the fire, marshmallows get soft and sticky.

88946.q: What is it called when water turns into ice?
88946.e: When liquid water becomes solid, it freezes. This happens when it is cold enough.
88946.m: When water turns into ice, it freezes.

88947.q: What do you get if you freeze squash in small moulds with a stick?
88947.e: The squash goes solid in the freezer. That makes a home-made ice lolly.
88947.m: Frozen squash becomes an ice lolly.

88948.q: Where does the same amount of water freeze faster?
88948.e: In a flat dish the water is only a thin layer and has a lot of surface. So it gives off its heat faster.
88948.m: Water freezes faster in a flat dish.

88949.q: Why are strawberries often soft and mushy after thawing?
88949.e: When fruit freezes, sharp ice crystals form inside it. They damage the cells, which is why the strawberries go soft when they thaw.
88949.m: Ice crystals make thawed strawberries soft.

88950.q: Which freezes over faster on a cold night?
88950.e: A puddle has little water, so it cools down quickly. A lot of water, on the other hand, cools only slowly.
88950.m: A small puddle freezes over faster than a lake.

88951.q: Why does a fast-flowing stream rarely freeze over completely in winter?
88951.e: In fast-flowing water, a solid layer of ice can hardly form. Still water freezes much more easily.
88951.m: Flowing water freezes over less easily than still water.

88952.q: What happens to wet washing hung outside in a hard frost?
88952.e: The water in the fabric freezes into ice. That is why the washing goes hard and stiff as a board.
88952.m: Wet washing freezes stiff in a frost.

88953.q: What do the stars on a freezer compartment show?
88953.e: The more stars a freezer compartment has, the colder it gets inside. With four stars you can freeze food for a long time.
88953.m: The stars on a freezer show how cold it gets.

88954.q: What is the thin white coating of ice called that forms on meadows and car roofs on cold nights?
88954.e: In a frost, moisture from the air freezes directly onto cold surfaces. This makes a fine white coating of ice crystals.
88954.m: Hoar frost is a fine coating of ice from frosty nights.

88955.q: Why is a blackboard that has been wiped wet dry again after a while?
88955.e: The thin layer of water on the board slowly goes into the air as invisible vapour. Then the board is dry again.
88955.m: The water on the blackboard evaporates.

88956.q: Why can you soon smell perfume all over the room?
88956.e: Perfume evaporates easily. The scented particles spread through the air and reach our nose.
88956.m: Evaporating perfume spreads through the air.

88957.q: How do you stop the water in a glass from getting less over several days?
a: Put the glass in the sun
88957.e: A lid closes the glass. So the water cannot escape into the room air as vapour.

88958.q: Which evaporates faster, water or cooking oil?
88958.e: At room temperature, water evaporates slowly but steadily. Cooking oil, on the other hand, hardly evaporates and stays for a long time.
88958.m: Water evaporates much faster than cooking oil.

88959.q: Why should you always put the cap back on a glue stick or felt-tip pen?
a: Otherwise it gets lighter in colour
88959.e: Glue and felt-tip pens contain liquid. Without a cap, it evaporates and the pen dries out.
88959.m: Pens dry out without a cap.

88960.q: What happens to wet footprints on warm tiles at the swimming pool?
88960.e: The warm tiles give the water heat. So it evaporates quickly and the prints disappear.
88960.m: Wet footprints on warm tiles disappear quickly.

88961.q: Why do you have to top up the water in a paddling pool in summer?
a: Some of it evaporates in the sun
The pool soaks up the water
The water gets heavier in the sun
88961.e: In the sun, some water evaporates every day. Together with splashes, there is less and less in the pool.
88961.m: Water evaporates from the paddling pool in the sun.

88962.q: Where do wet shoes dry fastest?
88962.e: Warmth and fresh air make the water in the shoe evaporate faster. In a bag, the moisture cannot escape.
88962.m: Wet shoes dry fastest somewhere warm and airy.

88963.q: Why does the bathroom mirror steam up after a shower?
88963.e: When you shower, a lot of water vapour gets into the air. On the cool mirror it turns back into tiny droplets.
88963.m: On the cool mirror, water vapour turns into droplets.

88964.q: What helps against a steamed-up car windscreen?
88964.e: The ventilation blows air onto the windscreen. This makes the droplets disappear and you can see clearly again.
88964.m: The ventilation clears a steamed-up windscreen.

88965.q: What happens to the mist on the bathroom mirror after a while?
88965.e: When the air gets drier, the tiny droplets evaporate again. Then the mirror is clear again.
88965.m: The mist on the mirror disappears over time.

88966.q: Where do drops collect on a pan lid while cooking?
88966.e: The steam from the pan rises to the lid. On its underside it cools down and turns into drops.
88966.m: Drops collect under the pan lid.

88967.q: Why do little icicles often hang from branches and fences after freezing rain?
88967.e: With freezing rain, rain falls on very cold branches and fences. As it drips off, it freezes at once into little icicles.
88967.m: After freezing rain, icicles hang from branches.

88968.q: What do you often see at the back of a car's exhaust on cold days?
88968.e: The exhaust gases contain water vapour. In the cold air it turns into tiny droplets and you see little white clouds.
88968.m: In winter you see little white clouds at the exhaust.

88969.q: What do you often find as droplets on the grass after a cool, clear night?
88969.e: At night the grass cools down a lot. Moisture from the air settles on it as fine droplets; this is called dew.
88969.m: Dewdrops form on the grass on cool nights.

88970.q: Why do some people breathe on their glasses before cleaning them?
a: The breath makes the glass slightly damp
The breath makes the glass hot
The breath makes the glass harder
88970.e: Warm breath contains water vapour. On the cooler glass it forms a damp film that makes smudges easier to wipe off.
88970.m: Glasses you have breathed on are easier to clean.

88971.q: How fast do snowflakes fall compared with raindrops?
a: They do not fall at all
88971.e: Snowflakes are light and have lots of little arms. The air slows them down a lot, so they float down slowly.
88971.m: Snowflakes fall more slowly than raindrops.

88972.q: What is trapped between the flakes of a fresh layer of snow?
88972.e: Fresh snow is loose and is mostly made of air. That is why it is so light and soft.

88973.q: What is snow called that the wind blows together into high heaps?
88973.e: Strong wind carries the snow along and drops it behind obstacles. This makes high snowdrifts.
88973.m: The wind can pile snow up into drifts.

88974.q: What do you call freshly fallen snow?
88974.e: Snow that has only just fallen is called new snow. It is loose and soft.
88974.m: Freshly fallen snow is called new snow.

88975.q: What is a good thing to look at snowflakes on before they melt?
a: The warm palm of your hand
88975.e: On cold, dark fabric, the flakes do not melt at once and stand out well. So you can see their delicate shapes.
88975.m: You can see snowflakes well on a cold, dark glove.

88976.q: What do you use to clear snow from the pavement in front of the house?
88976.e: With the wide snow shovel you push the snow aside. So the path is clear again.
88976.m: You clear snow with a snow shovel.

88977.q: What happens to a snowflake that lands on your warm hand?
a: It stays there for a long time
88977.e: Your hand is warm. This quickly turns the little snowflake into a drop of water.
88977.m: A snowflake melts on a warm hand.

88978.q: Why do skiers like to wear ski goggles when it is snowing?
a: So no flakes fly into their eyes
88978.e: When it snows and you are moving fast, flakes fly into your face. Ski goggles protect your eyes and you see better.
88978.m: Ski goggles protect your eyes from snowflakes.

88979.q: Where do icicles often hang on village fountains in winter?
a: On the bottom of the trough
In the water of the trough
88979.e: Water constantly splashes and drips from the fountain spout. In a frost it freezes into icicles there.
88979.m: Icicles often form on the fountain spout.

88980.q: Why should you not suck icicles from the roof?
88980.e: The meltwater flows over the roof and picks up dirt. This dirt then ends up in the icicle too.
88980.m: Icicles from the roof can be dirty.

88981.q: What do icicles and stalactites have in common?
88981.e: With both, water drips down and leaves something behind. With an icicle it is freezing water, with a stalactite it is limestone.
88981.m: Icicles and stalactites grow from drips.

88982.q: What do you often see at the tip of a growing icicle?
88982.e: The water runs down the icicle and collects at the tip. A drop often hangs there before it freezes or falls.
88982.m: A drop often hangs at the tip of an icicle.

88983.q: How long can icicles on roofs get?
88983.e: In long cold spells with lots of meltwater, icicles keep growing. Some get longer than a metre.
88983.m: Icicles can be more than a metre long.

88984.q: What is often left when a muddy puddle has dried up?
88984.e: The water disappears, but the soil in it stays behind. It dries into a cracked layer of mud.
88984.m: Dried-up puddles leave dry mud behind.

88985.q: What is best to wear for jumping in puddles?
88985.e: Wellies are tall and watertight. So your feet stay dry when you jump in puddles.
88985.m: You wear wellies for jumping in puddles.

88986.q: What do you hear when you jump into a puddle?
88986.e: When you jump, the water is suddenly pushed away and splashes up. This makes a splashing sound.
88986.m: Jumping in a puddle goes splash.

88987.q: What do birds often do at a puddle?
88987.e: For many birds, a puddle is a little bath and a place to drink. They drink from it and clean their feathers.
88987.m: Birds like to bathe and drink at puddles.

88988.q: What do you call a small, still pool of water in the woods that is bigger than a puddle?
88988.e: A pond like this is a small, shallow body of water. It can dry up in summer and is important for frogs and newts.
88988.m: A pond is a small, still body of water.

88989.q: Why should you ride slowly through a big puddle on your bike?
a: You cannot see how deep it is
88989.e: A hole or a stone may be hidden under the water. If you ride slowly, you are less likely to fall.

88990.q: Why does it splash when a car drives through a puddle?
a: The wheels push the water away
The water is as light as air
88990.e: The heavy wheels push the water quickly aside. It splashes up, which is why you keep your distance at the roadside.
88990.m: Car wheels push puddle water aside.

88991.q: Why are there often especially many puddles after a thunderstorm?
a: A lot of rain falls in a short time
88991.e: In thunderstorms, a lot of rain often falls at once. The ground cannot soak up so much water quickly enough.
88991.m: Heavy storm rain makes lots of puddles.

88992.q: What do you see when water is boiling hard in a pan?
88992.e: At the hot bottom of the pan, water turns into steam. The steam bubbles rise and make the water bubble.
88992.m: Boiling water bubbles with big bubbles.

88993.q: What does a kettle do as soon as the water boils?
88993.e: A kettle has a switch inside that reacts to the steam. When the water boils, the appliance switches off.
88993.m: A kettle switches itself off when the water boils.

88994.q: Why do you turn the pan handle inwards when cooking?
a: So nobody pulls the pan down
88994.e: A handle sticking out over the edge of the cooker can easily be knocked. Then hot water could fall down and scald someone.
88994.m: For safety, turn pan handles inwards.

88995.q: What happens to pasta in boiling water?
88995.e: The hard, dry pasta takes up water in the hot water. As it does, it gets soft and bigger.
88995.m: Pasta gets soft in boiling water.

88996.q: What can happen if a pan of boiling water is too full?
88996.e: The rising bubbles lift the water. If the pan is too full, it runs over the edge.
88996.m: A pan that is too full boils over.

88997.q: What happens to water that you leave boiling for a very long time?
88997.e: While it boils, water keeps turning into steam and escaping. If you let it boil too long, the pan is empty at some point.
88997.m: Boiling water gets less over time.

88998.q: What do you do if the water in the pan is bubbling too hard?
a: Put ice cubes on the cooker
88998.e: With less heat, fewer steam bubbles form. The water then boils more gently and does not splash.
88998.m: If it bubbles too hard, turn the heat down.

88999.q: Why should you not pour boiling water into a thin, cold glass?
88999.e: The glass suddenly gets hot inside while staying cold outside. This can make it crack and shatter.
88999.m: Boiling water can crack a cold glass.

89000.q: What do you hear just before the water in a kettle boils?
89000.e: Steam bubbles form at the hot bottom and collapse again at first. This makes a rushing sound.
89000.m: Just before boiling, the water makes a rushing sound.

89001.e: The sun warms the air. Then the droplets evaporate and the fog disappears.
89001.m: The sun can clear the fog.

89002.q: What do ships use to warn each other in thick fog?
89002.e: A foghorn makes a very loud, deep sound. So other ships can hear where you are, even if they cannot see anything.
89002.m: In fog, ships warn each other with a foghorn.

89003.q: What makes a spider's web easy to see on a foggy morning?
89003.e: The tiny droplets from the fog settle on the threads. Then the whole web glistens.
89003.m: Fog droplets make spiders' webs visible.

89004.q: What is sometimes difficult at an airport in very thick fog?
89004.e: In thick fog, pilots find it hard to see the runway. That is why there are sometimes delays.
89004.m: Thick fog makes take-offs and landings harder.

89005.q: Which lights on a car are specially meant for fog?
89005.e: Front fog lights sit low on the car and shine widely onto the road. At the back, a bright red rear fog light makes the car easier to see.

89006.q: What is very light, thin fog called that you can still see quite far through?
89006.e: Haze is like a fine veil in the air. It is much less dense than real fog.
89006.m: Haze is a thin, light fog.

89007.q: Where does fog often form in the morning?
89007.e: The air over water is especially damp. When it cools down at night, patches of fog often form there.
89007.m: Fog often forms over lakes and rivers.

89008.q: What should drivers do with the distance to the car in front when it is foggy?
89008.e: In fog you spot obstacles late. With more distance there is enough time to brake.

89109.q: Which small mountain lake is traditionally seen as the source of the Rhine?
89109.e: Lake Toma (Lai da Tuma in Romansh) is a small mountain lake at the very top of the Surselva. It has long been seen as the source of the Vorderrhein and so of the Rhine.
89109.m: Lake Toma is seen as the source of the Rhine.

89110.q: In which canton is Lake Toma, the source of the Rhine?
89110.e: Lake Toma lies at the top of the Vorderrhein valley in the municipality of Tujetsch in the Grisons. The village of Sedrun also belongs to Tujetsch.
89110.m: The source of the Rhine is in the Grisons.

89111.q: At roughly what height is Lake Toma?
89111.e: Lake Toma lies at about 2344 m above sea level. From there to the North Sea, the Rhine travels more than 1200 km.
89111.m: The Rhine starts high up at over 2300 metres.

89112.q: Near which Alpine pass is Lake Toma?
89112.e: Lake Toma lies south of the Oberalp Pass, below the Badus. From the pass you can hike to the source in about two hours.
89112.m: You can hike from the Oberalp Pass to the source of the Rhine.

89113.q: Where do the Vorderrhein and the Hinterrhein flow together?
89113.e: At Reichenau in the municipality of Tamins, the two headwaters join. Only from there is the river simply called the Rhine.
89113.m: At Reichenau, the Vorderrhein and Hinterrhein become the Rhine.

a: In the Rheinwald below the Rheinwaldhorn
89114.e: The Hinterrhein rises in the high valley of Rheinwald below the Rheinwaldhorn. It then flows north through the Via Mala.
89114.m: The Hinterrhein comes from the Rheinwald.

89115.q: Because of its pale, steep walls, what is the Ruinaulta Rhine gorge in the Grisons also called?
89115.e: Between Ilanz and Reichenau, the Vorderrhein has cut deep into huge amounts of rock debris. The pale, steep walls are reminiscent of the Grand Canyon in the USA.
89115.m: The Ruinaulta is the Rhine gorge in the Grisons.

89116.q: Which enormous event about 10,000 years ago made the Ruinaulta Rhine gorge possible?
89116.e: In the Flims landslide, billions of cubic metres of rock crashed into the valley. It is considered the largest known landslide in the Alps.
89116.m: The Flims landslide is the largest known landslide in the Alps.

89117.q: Which large lake does the Rhine flow through before it reaches the Rhine Falls?
89117.e: The Alpine Rhine flows into Lake Constance. At Stein am Rhein it leaves the lake as the High Rhine.
89117.m: The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.

89118.q: In which city does the Rhine make the “Rhine knee” and turn north?
89118.e: In Basel, the Rhine turns north in a great curve. The Middle Bridge is seen as the boundary between the High Rhine and the Upper Rhine.
89118.m: The Rhine makes its knee in Basel.

89119.q: Why are the Rhine ports in Basel important for Switzerland?
a: They link Switzerland to the sea by ship
Salt from the sea is obtained there
All the Alpine passes end there
89119.e: From Basel, the Rhine can be used by large cargo ships all the way to the North Sea. This gives Switzerland a waterway to the sea.
89119.m: Through the Basel Rhine ports, Switzerland is linked to the sea.

89120.q: Which river is the tributary of the Rhine that carries the most water?
89120.e: The Aare drains large parts of the Central Plateau and the Alps. At Koblenz in Aargau it even carries more water than the Rhine itself.
89120.m: The Aare is the Rhine’s tributary with the most water.

89121.q: Which countries border the canton of St Gallen on the eastern side along the Alpine Rhine?
89121.e: The Alpine Rhine forms the border between the canton of St Gallen and Liechtenstein and, further north, Austria. After that it flows into Lake Constance.
89121.m: The Alpine Rhine separates Switzerland from Liechtenstein and Austria.

89122.q: What is the section of the Rhine between Lake Constance and Basel called?
89122.e: The High Rhine flows from Lake Constance to Basel and mostly forms the border with Germany. From Basel it is called the Upper Rhine.
89122.m: The High Rhine flows between Lake Constance and Basel.

89123.q: Which cantonal capital does the Rhône flow past in Valais?
89123.e: Sion (Sitten in German) is the capital of the canton of Valais and lies in the Rhône valley. The castle hills of Valère and Tourbillon tower above the town.
89123.m: The Valais capital Sion lies on the Rhône.

89124.q: Roughly how long is the Rhône?
89124.e: The Rhône is just over 800 km long. About a third of it is in Switzerland, the rest in France.
89124.m: The Rhône is about 800 kilometres long.

89125.q: What is the Rhône called in German in Upper Valais?
89125.e: In German-speaking Upper Valais, the Rhône is called Rotten, or “Rottu” in dialect. In Lower Valais it is called the Rhône.
89125.m: In Upper Valais, the Rhône is called Rotten.

89126.q: In which city does the Arve flow into the Rhône?
89126.e: In Geneva, the Arve from the Mont Blanc area flows into the Rhône. At the spot called “La Jonction” you can see the cloudy Arve water next to the clear Rhône water.
89126.m: The Rhône and the Arve meet in Geneva.

89127.q: What are the big building projects called that have been taming the Rhône in Valais since the 19th century?
89127.e: The first Rhône correction began in 1863, the second in 1930. The third Rhône correction is meant to protect Valais better from floods and give the Rhône more space.
89127.m: Rhône corrections protect Valais from floods.

89128.q: In which French city does the Saône flow into the Rhône?
89128.e: In Lyon, the Saône and the Rhône flow together. After that, the Rhône flows south to the Mediterranean.
89128.m: The Rhône and the Saône join in Lyon.

89129.q: Which valley in the Grisons does the Inn flow through?
89129.e: The Inn flows through the Upper and Lower Engadine. The name Engadine is often explained as “garden of the Inn”.
89129.m: The Inn is the river of the Engadine.

89130.q: Which national park lies in the Lower Engadine near the Inn?
89130.e: The Swiss National Park was founded in 1914 and is the only national park in Switzerland. It lies near Zernez in the Lower Engadine.
89130.m: The Swiss National Park is in the Engadine.

89132.q: Near which pass does the Inn rise?
89132.e: The Inn rises at Lake Lunghin by the Lunghin Pass, near the Maloja Pass. From there it flows north-east through the Engadine.
89132.m: The Inn rises near the Maloja Pass.

89133.q: Which lakes in the Upper Engadine does the Inn flow through?
89133.e: After its source, the Inn flows through Lake Sils, Lake Silvaplana, Lake Champfèr and Lake St Moritz. These lakes shape the Upper Engadine.
89133.m: In the Upper Engadine, the Inn flows through a chain of lakes.

89134.q: Which Austrian state capital does the Inn flow through?
89134.e: After Switzerland, the Inn flows through Tyrol. Innsbruck is even named after the bridge over the Inn.
89134.m: Innsbruck has the Inn in its name.

89135.q: Near which pass does the river Ticino rise?
89135.e: The Ticino rises at the Nufenen Pass and first flows through the Bedretto valley. Then it follows the Leventina southwards.
89135.m: The Ticino rises at the Nufenen Pass.

89136.q: Which canton is named after the river Ticino?
89136.e: The canton of Ticino bears the name of its most important river.
89136.m: The canton of Ticino is named after its river.

89137.q: Which lake does the Ticino flow into?
89137.e: The Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore between Locarno and Bellinzona. Later it leaves the lake again in Italy.
89137.m: The Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore.

89138.q: Which large Italian river does the Ticino flow into?
89138.e: The Ticino leaves Lake Maggiore at Sesto Calende and flows into the Po near Pavia. The Po is the longest river in Italy.
89138.m: The Ticino is a tributary of the Po.

89139.q: Which long valley does the Ticino flow through between Airolo and Biasca?
89139.e: The Leventina is the main valley of upper Ticino. The Gotthard motorway and the Gotthard railway also run through it.
89139.m: The Ticino flows through the Leventina.

89140.q: Which cantonal capital in Ticino does the river Ticino flow through?
89140.e: Bellinzona lies on the Ticino between Biasca and Lake Maggiore. The town’s three castles are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

89141.q: Roughly how big is Lake Geneva?
89141.e: Lake Geneva has an area of about 580 km². That makes it a little bigger than Lake Constance.
89141.m: Lake Geneva covers about 580 square kilometres.

89142.q: Roughly how deep is Lake Geneva at its deepest point?
89142.e: The deepest point, about 310 m, lies between Lausanne and Évian. That makes it one of the deepest lakes in Switzerland.
89142.m: Lake Geneva is up to 310 metres deep.

89143.q: Which country shares Lake Geneva with Switzerland?
89143.e: Most of the south shore belongs to the French département of Haute-Savoie. About 60 per cent of the lake’s area belongs to Switzerland.
89143.m: Switzerland and France share Lake Geneva.

89144.q: Roughly how high does the Jet d’eau in Lake Geneva shoot?
89144.e: The Jet d’eau in Geneva shoots water up to 140 m into the air. It is a landmark of the city.
89144.m: Geneva’s Jet d’eau shoots up to 140 metres high.

89145.q: Which vineyard terraces on Lake Geneva are a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
89145.e: Lavaux lies between Lausanne and Vevey on the north shore. Its steep terraces have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
89145.m: The vineyard terraces of Lavaux are World Heritage.

89146.q: Which famous castle stands on the water’s edge of Lake Geneva near Montreux?
89146.e: Chillon Castle stands on a rock in the lake at Veytaux near Montreux. It is one of the most visited historic monuments in Switzerland.
89146.m: Chillon Castle stands right in Lake Geneva.

89147.q: Which three cantons have a shore on Lake Geneva?
89147.e: Vaud has the long north shore, Geneva the south-western tip and Valais a small part in the east. The rest of the south shore is French.
89147.m: The cantons of Geneva, Vaud and Valais lie on Lake Geneva.

89148.q: Which river flows through Lake Thun?
89148.e: The Aare comes from Lake Brienz, flows through Lake Thun and leaves it at Thun. Then it flows towards Bern.
89148.m: The Aare flows through Lake Thun.

89149.q: Which town lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz?
89149.e: Interlaken means “between the lakes”. The town lies on the plain between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.

89150.q: How was the basin of Lake Thun formed?
89150.e: In the ice ages, the Aare glacier flowed through the valley. It carved out a deep basin that later filled with water.
89150.m: Lake Thun lies in a basin carved out by a glacier.

89151.q: From which lake does the Aare flow into Lake Thun?
89151.e: The Aare first flows through Lake Brienz. At Interlaken it flows on into Lake Thun.
89151.m: The Aare flows from Lake Brienz into Lake Thun.

89152.q: Which caves lie high above the north shore of Lake Thun?
89152.e: The St Beatus Caves are named after Saint Beatus, who is said to have lived there. You can visit them on paths.
89152.m: The St Beatus Caves lie above Lake Thun.

89153.q: Which castle with a church lies on a peninsula on the south shore of Lake Thun?
89153.e: Spiez Castle stands with its Romanesque church above Spiez bay. It is one of the best-known views of Lake Thun.
89153.m: Spiez Castle towers above a bay of Lake Thun.

89154.q: Roughly how much of Lake Maggiore belongs to Switzerland?
89154.e: About 20 per cent of the lake’s area is in the canton of Ticino. Most of it belongs to Italy.
89154.m: Lake Maggiore lies mostly in Italy.

89155.q: Which town in Ticino lies at the northern end of Lake Maggiore?
89155.e: Locarno lies on the north shore of the lake. The old town with the Piazza Grande is known for the film festival.

89156.q: Which islands in the Swiss part of Lake Maggiore have a botanical garden?
89156.e: On the Brissago Islands, plants from many warm regions of the world grow. You reach them by boat, for example from Brissago or Locarno.
89156.m: Plants from all over the world grow on the Brissago Islands.

89157.q: Roughly how deep is Lake Maggiore at its deepest point?
89157.e: Lake Maggiore is up to 372 m deep. Its bottom therefore lies well below sea level.
89157.m: The bottom of Lake Maggiore lies below sea level.

89158.q: Roughly how long is Lake Maggiore?
89158.e: Lake Maggiore is about 64 km long but only up to 10 km wide. It reaches from Ticino far into Italy.
89158.m: Lake Maggiore is a long, narrow lake.

89159.q: Where does Lake Maggiore rank among Italy’s largest lakes?
89159.e: By area, only Lake Garda is bigger in Italy. Lake Maggiore comes second.
89159.m: Only Lake Garda is bigger in Italy than Lake Maggiore.

89160.q: Which famous group of islands off Stresa lies in the Italian part of Lake Maggiore?
89160.e: The Borromean Islands with Isola Bella lie off Stresa and Verbania. They are known for their palaces and gardens.
89160.m: The Borromean Islands lie in the Italian part of the lake.

89161.q: What does a river build its delta from?
a: From sand, gravel and mud that it brings with it
From ice that freezes in the sea
From salt that comes from the sea
89161.e: Where a river flows into a lake or the sea, it slows down. There it deposits sand, gravel and mud, and the delta grows.
89161.m: A delta forms from material deposited by the river.

89162.q: Which Greek letter is a river delta named after?
89162.e: Many deltas are roughly triangular. That is why they remind people of the Greek capital letter delta (Δ).
89162.m: The delta is named after the triangular Greek letter.

89163.q: Which river forms a famous delta in Egypt on the Mediterranean?
89163.e: The Nile Delta north of Cairo is one of the best-known deltas in the world. The Greek historian Herodotus already compared its shape to the letter delta.
89163.m: The Nile Delta is in Egypt on the Mediterranean.

89164.q: Which river has built a large delta into Lake Maggiore between Locarno and Ascona?
89164.e: The Maggia brings a lot of gravel from the Maggia valley. Its delta reaches far out into the lake and separates Locarno from Ascona.
89164.m: The Maggia has built a large delta near Locarno.

89165.q: At which end of Lake Geneva is the Rhône building its delta?
a: At the western end near Geneva
On the north shore near Nyon
89165.e: The Rhône comes from Valais and flows into the eastern end of Lake Geneva. There it deposits the material from the Valais Alps.
89165.m: The Rhône builds a delta at the eastern end of Lake Geneva.

89166.q: What is the delta of the Rhône on the Mediterranean called?
89166.e: The Camargue lies south of Arles between the mouths of the Rhône. It is known for its flamingos and white horses.
89166.m: The Camargue is the Rhône delta.

89167.q: In which country is the large delta of the Rhine and the Meuse?
89167.e: In the Netherlands, the Rhine and the Meuse split into many branches. The large port of Rotterdam also lies in this delta.
89167.m: The Rhine delta is in the Netherlands.

89169.q: What is the gently sloping bank on the inside of a river bend called?
89169.e: On the inside, the water flows slowly and deposits gravel and sand. A gently sloping bank forms there: the slip-off slope.
89169.m: On the slip-off slope, the river deposits sand and gravel.

89170.q: What do you call a cut-off river loop that water no longer flows through?
89170.e: When a river breaks through a narrow loop, the old bend is left behind as still water. Such oxbow lakes are valuable habitats.
89170.m: A cut-off meander becomes an oxbow lake.

89171.q: At Rheinau in the canton of Zurich, the Rhine winds in two large loops. What are such river loops called?
89171.e: At Rheinau, the Rhine forms a double river loop. Such loops are called meanders.
89171.m: At Rheinau, the Rhine makes a double loop.

89172.q: Which river in the Jura makes a large loop at Saint-Ursanne and then flows back into France?
89172.e: The Doubs flows from France into the canton of Jura, makes a big loop and returns to France. This loop is called the Clos du Doubs.
89172.m: The Doubs makes a large loop in the Jura.

89173.q: Why are there only a few natural meanders left in Switzerland today?
a: Many rivers were straightened and embanked
89173.e: In the 19th and 20th centuries, many rivers were straightened to gain land and carry away floodwater. Today some stretches are being restored to nature again.
89173.m: Straightened rivers have lost their loops.

a: An area by a river that is flooded again and again
A glacier in the high mountains
89174.e: Floodplains lie along rivers and streams. They are regularly flooded when the water is high and then dry out again.
89174.m: Floodplains are flooded by their river again and again.

89175.q: Which trees are typical of the softwood floodplain close to the river?
89175.e: Willows and poplars can cope with long floods and grow quickly. They form the softwood floodplain right by the water.
89175.m: Willows and poplars grow in the softwood floodplain.

89176.q: Why are floodplains valuable for flood protection?
a: They take in water and slow down the flood wave
They make the water drain away faster
They divert the water into the sea
89176.e: In a floodplain, a river can spread out during a flood. The water is held back, and water levels further downstream rise less.

89177.q: Why are the Bolle di Magadino on Lake Maggiore an important nature reserve?
a: Many migrating birds rest there in the floodplain
The highest mountain in Ticino is there
There is a large glacier there
89177.e: The Bolle di Magadino are a floodplain and wetland where the Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore. Many migrating birds stop there on their journey.
89177.m: The Bolle di Magadino are a floodplain on Lake Maggiore.

89178.q: Switzerland’s most valuable floodplains have been protected by the federal government since 1992. What must the cantons do with them?
a: Preserve them and improve them where possible
Drain them and build on them
89178.e: The most important floodplains are listed in a federal inventory. The cantons must preserve them and, where possible, make them more natural again.
89178.m: Switzerland’s most valuable floodplains are under federal protection.

89179.q: Which animal, now back at home in Switzerland, helps shape floodplains with its dams?
89179.e: The beaver had died out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1956. With its dams it blocks streams and creates new wetlands.
89179.m: The beaver builds dams and shapes floodplains.

89180.q: What is special about the Pfyn forest in Valais?
a: The Rhône still flows largely freely there
The largest glacier in the Alps is there
The highest dam in the world is there
There is a large sand desert there
89180.e: In the Pfyn forest between Leuk and Sierre, the Rhône may still split into branches and form gravel banks. This has become rare in Valais.
89180.m: In the Pfyn forest, the Rhône still flows wild.

89181.q: Why do especially many kinds of animals and plants live in floodplains?
a: Floods keep creating new, varied habitats
It is dry there all year round
The ground is the same everywhere
89181.e: Floods deposit gravel, sweep away trees and create pools. This forms a patchwork of wet, dry, young and old habitats.
89181.m: Thanks to floods, floodplains are very rich in species.

a: Groundwater flowing underground through gravel and sand
A river in a cave with boats
A stream that only flows in winter
89182.e: In the gravel layers of many valleys, groundwater slowly flows down the valley. This underground river is called a groundwater stream.
89182.m: A groundwater stream flows unseen through gravel and sand.

89184.q: How fast does groundwater typically flow in gravel?
89184.e: Groundwater has to squeeze through the spaces between grains of gravel and sand. So it flows very slowly, often only a few metres a day.

89185.q: What do you call a rock layer in which groundwater can collect and flow?
89185.e: Gravel and sand have lots of spaces and let water through well. Such layers are called aquifers.
89185.m: Gravel and sand make good aquifers.

89186.q: Which type of soil lets almost no water through and holds back groundwater?
89186.e: Clay is made of tiny particles with very small pores. Water hardly gets through, so clay often forms the bottom of an aquifer.
89186.m: Layers of clay hold back groundwater.

89187.q: Where does a groundwater stream mainly get new water from?
a: From rain and river water soaking in
From inside the Earth through volcanoes
89187.e: Rain and meltwater soak into the ground. In many valleys, water from the river also seeps into the groundwater.
89187.m: Rain and rivers top up the groundwater.

89188.q: Why are there protection zones around places where groundwater is taken?
a: So that the drinking water stays clean
So that nobody goes hiking there
So that the water stays warmer
So that animals do not drink there
89188.e: Strict rules apply in protection zones, for example for fertiliser or buildings. This stops harmful substances getting into the groundwater.
89188.m: Protection zones keep drinking water clean.

89189.q: What do you call the place where groundwater comes to the surface by itself?
89189.e: Where a water-bearing layer meets the surface, groundwater comes out as a spring. Many municipalities use spring water as drinking water.
89189.m: At a spring, groundwater comes out of the ground by itself.

89190.q: What is the upper limit of groundwater in the ground called?
89190.e: The water table shows up to what height the ground is filled with water. In dry periods it falls, and after a lot of rain it rises.
89190.m: The water table rises and falls with the weather.

89191.q: What is the section of the Rhine from Reichenau to Lake Constance called?
89191.e: From the confluence at Reichenau, the Alpine Rhine flows through the Rhine valleys of the Grisons and St Gallen. It ends in Lake Constance.
89191.m: The Alpine Rhine flows from Reichenau into Lake Constance.

89192.q: Which cantonal capital does the Rhine flow past in the Rhine valley of the Grisons?
89192.e: Chur lies in the Rhine valley, where the Plessur flows into the Rhine. Chur is considered the oldest town in Switzerland.

89193.q: At which town in Valais does the Rhône turn north in a bend?
89193.e: As far as Martigny, the Rhône flows south-west. There it turns sharply north and flows towards Lake Geneva.
89193.m: At Martigny, the Rhône makes a bend.

89195.q: Which river in Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore?
89195.e: The Ticino rises in the area of the Nufenen Pass, flows through the Leventina and past Bellinzona, and enters Lake Maggiore near Locarno.
89195.m: The Ticino flows into Lake Maggiore.

89196.q: Which river is piling up a large delta at the south-eastern end of Lake Constance?
89196.e: Every year, the Alpine Rhine brings large amounts of gravel, sand and mud into Lake Constance. So its delta keeps growing out into the lake.
89196.m: The Rhine is building a growing delta in Lake Constance.

89197.q: At roughly what height is the surface of Lake Geneva?
89197.e: Lake Geneva lies at about 372 m above sea level. That is clearly lower than most lakes in the Central Plateau.
89197.m: Lake Geneva lies at about 372 metres above sea level.

89198.q: Where are rivers most likely to form meanders?
a: In flat land with little slope
In narrow rocky gorges in the high mountains
89198.e: With little slope, the water flows slowly and swerves to the side. Over time, wide loops form.

89199.q: What is the chemical formula of the substance that gives hydrochloric acid when dissolved in water?
89199.e: Hydrochloric acid is a solution of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in water. HCl is made of one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom.
89199.m: Hydrochloric acid is hydrogen chloride, HCl, dissolved in water.

89200.q: Why do you wear safety goggles when working with hydrochloric acid?
89200.e: Hydrochloric acid attacks skin and eyes. Splashes can seriously injure the eyes, so safety goggles are a must.
89200.m: Hydrochloric acid is corrosive and dangerous for the eyes.

89201.q: What do you see when you put a piece of zinc in dilute hydrochloric acid?
89201.e: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid, producing hydrogen gas that rises as bubbles. The zinc slowly dissolves.
89201.m: Base metals such as zinc react with hydrochloric acid and form hydrogen.

89202.q: Which of these metals is not attacked by hydrochloric acid?
89202.e: Gold is a precious metal and does not react with hydrochloric acid. Base metals such as zinc, magnesium or iron, on the other hand, dissolve in it.
89202.m: Precious metals such as gold are not attacked by hydrochloric acid.

89203.q: Why do you often see white fumes above open, concentrated hydrochloric acid?
a: Hydrogen chloride escapes and forms tiny droplets with moisture in the air
The acid burns in the air
The acid evaporates as pure water
89203.e: Hydrogen chloride gas escapes from concentrated hydrochloric acid. With the water vapour in the air it forms tiny acid droplets that can be seen as a mist.
89203.m: Concentrated hydrochloric acid fumes because hydrogen chloride escapes.

89204.q: Which particles make hydrochloric acid acidic?
89204.e: In water, HCl gives up a hydrogen ion, which joins a water molecule to form an oxonium ion (H3O+). These ions make every acidic solution acidic.
89204.m: Acidic solutions contain lots of oxonium ions.

89205.q: What is dilute hydrochloric acid sometimes used for on building sites?
a: To remove cement and lime residues
89205.e: Hydrochloric acid dissolves deposits containing lime, such as cement haze on tiles. Gloves and safety goggles must be worn.
89205.m: Dilute hydrochloric acid dissolves residues containing lime.

89206.q: What colour does blue litmus paper turn when dipped in hydrochloric acid?
89206.e: Litmus turns red in acidic solutions. Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, so it clearly turns the paper red.
89206.m: Acids turn blue litmus paper red.

89208.q: What is the chemical formula of sulphuric acid?
89208.e: One molecule of sulphuric acid contains two hydrogen atoms, one sulphur atom and four oxygen atoms.
89208.m: Sulphuric acid has the formula H2SO4.

89209.q: Why is sulphuric acid called a diprotic acid?
a: It can give up two hydrogen ions
It reacts with only two metals
89209.e: A molecule of H2SO4 has two hydrogen atoms that it can give up as hydrogen ions. Hydrochloric acid, on the other hand, can only give up one.
89209.m: Sulphuric acid can give up two hydrogen ions per molecule.

89210.q: What must you remember when diluting concentrated sulphuric acid?
a: Always pour the acid into the water, never the other way round
Always pour the water into the acid
Pour both into a glass at the same time
89210.e: A great deal of heat is released when they mix. If you pour water into the acid, it can suddenly boil and spray corrosive acid around.
89210.m: Do what you oughta, add acid to water.

89211.q: What happens when you pour concentrated sulphuric acid onto sugar?
a: The sugar turns black and carbon forms
89211.e: Concentrated sulphuric acid pulls the water out of the sugar. What remains is a black, puffed-up mass of carbon.
89211.m: Concentrated sulphuric acid strongly removes water.

89212.q: In which part of a car do you find sulphuric acid?
89212.e: The classic car battery is a lead-acid battery. Its lead plates stand in dilute sulphuric acid.
89212.m: Lead-acid car batteries contain dilute sulphuric acid.

89213.q: Which gas is an important starting material for making sulphuric acid?
89213.e: Sulphur is burnt to sulphur dioxide, which is then further oxidised to sulphur trioxide. With water this becomes sulphuric acid.
89213.m: Sulphuric acid is made from sulphur dioxide.

89214.q: What is a large part of the sulphuric acid produced worldwide used for?
a: As an additive in drinking water
89214.e: Sulphuric acid is one of the most produced chemicals in the world. Much of it is used to make phosphate fertiliser.
89214.m: Sulphuric acid is an important raw material for fertilisers.

89215.q: Which hazard symbol is on a bottle of concentrated sulphuric acid?
89215.e: Concentrated sulphuric acid destroys skin, eyes and many materials. The pictogram shows drops attacking a hand and a surface.
89215.m: Concentrated sulphuric acid is highly corrosive.

89216.q: Which well-known building material is chemically a salt of sulphuric acid?
89216.e: Gypsum is calcium sulphate with built-in water. So it is one of the salts of sulphuric acid.
89216.m: Gypsum is a calcium salt of sulphuric acid.

89217.q: Which substance is dissolved in water when people talk about sodium hydroxide solution?
89217.e: Sodium hydroxide solution forms when solid sodium hydroxide (NaOH) is dissolved in water. The solution gets warm.
89217.m: Sodium hydroxide solution is sodium hydroxide dissolved in water.

89218.q: What is the formula of sodium hydroxide?
89218.e: Sodium hydroxide is made of sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH-). Hence the formula NaOH.
89218.m: Sodium hydroxide has the formula NaOH.

89219.q: Why should you not keep sodium hydroxide solution in an aluminium container?
a: Sodium hydroxide attacks and dissolves aluminium
Aluminium turns the solution into water
89219.e: Aluminium reacts with sodium hydroxide solution: the metal dissolves and hydrogen gas forms. That is why alkalis are kept in plastic bottles.

89220.q: Why does a pretzel have a shiny brown crust?
a: It got a dip in dilute sodium hydroxide solution before baking
Someone sprayed sugar water on it
89220.e: The dough is dipped briefly in dilute sodium hydroxide solution. During baking this creates the typical brown crust, and the alkali becomes harmless.
89220.m: Pretzels get their brown crust from a dip in dilute sodium hydroxide solution.

89221.q: What does a dilute alkali feel like on the skin?
89221.e: Alkalis attack the fats and proteins in the skin. This makes the skin feel soapy; you should rinse it off at once with plenty of water.
89221.m: Alkalis feel soapy on the skin and must be washed off at once.

89222.q: Why must you always wear safety goggles when working with sodium hydroxide solution?
a: Alkalis can badly burn the eyes
89222.e: Even small splashes of alkali can permanently damage the cornea of the eye. Alkalis are often even more dangerous to the eyes than acids.
89222.m: Safety goggles protect your eyes when working with alkalis.

89223.q: Which household product often contains sodium hydroxide?
89223.e: Drain cleaners often contain sodium hydroxide. It breaks down hair and fat that block the drain.
89223.m: Drain cleaners often contain corrosive sodium hydroxide.

89224.q: What do you notice when you dissolve solid sodium hydroxide in water?
89224.e: Dissolving sodium hydroxide in water releases a lot of heat. That is why the pellets are added to the water only slowly.
89224.m: Dissolving sodium hydroxide in water releases heat.

89225.q: What happens to solid sodium hydroxide pellets left open in the air?
a: They draw water from the air and become damp
They become stone hard and shiny
89225.e: Sodium hydroxide is hygroscopic, which means it takes in moisture from the air. That is why it is kept tightly sealed.
89225.m: Sodium hydroxide draws moisture from the air.

89226.q: What is an indicator in chemistry?
a: A substance whose colour shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline
A substance that makes acids harmless
89226.e: Indicators are dyes that change colour depending on the pH. This lets you tell without a measuring device whether something is acidic, neutral or alkaline.
89226.m: An indicator's colour shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.

89227.q: What colour does red cabbage juice turn in a strongly alkaline solution?
89227.e: The dye in red cabbage changes as the pH rises. In strongly alkaline solutions it turns green and finally yellow.
89227.m: Red cabbage juice turns green to yellow in strong alkalis.

89228.q: What colour is litmus in a neutral solution?
89228.e: Litmus is red in acidic solutions and blue in alkaline ones. In the neutral range it shows a mixed colour, namely violet.
89228.m: Litmus is violet in neutral solutions.

89229.q: What colour does red cabbage juice turn when you add vinegar?
89229.e: Vinegar is acidic. In acidic solutions the red cabbage dye turns red.
89229.m: Red cabbage juice turns red in acidic solutions.

89230.q: What colour is phenolphthalein in an alkali?
89230.e: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic and neutral solutions. In alkalis it turns pink to violet.
89230.m: Phenolphthalein only turns pink in alkalis.

89231.q: Which garden plant has blue or pink flowers depending on how acidic the soil is?
89231.e: In acidic soil the hydrangea can take up more aluminium and then has blue flowers. In soil with lime, which is less acidic, it tends to flower pink.
89231.m: The flower colour of many hydrangeas depends on how acidic the soil is.

89232.q: What is the dye litmus obtained from?
89232.e: Litmus is a mixture of dyes obtained from certain lichens. It is one of the oldest indicators.
89232.m: The indicator litmus comes from lichens.

89233.q: Why does black tea get lighter when you add lemon juice?
a: The tea dyes act as an indicator and change colour in acid
The lemon juice dilutes the tea a lot
89233.e: Some dyes in black tea react to acid. In acidic conditions the tea therefore looks lighter.
89233.m: Black tea gets lighter with acid because its dyes act as an indicator.

89234.q: What is special about universal indicator?
a: It shows the approximate pH with many colour steps
It only works with hydrochloric acid
89234.e: Universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. That is why it changes colour in many steps across the whole pH range.
89234.m: Universal indicator shows the pH with many colour steps.

89235.q: Which pH value best matches lemon juice?
89235.e: Lemon juice is clearly acidic. With universal indicator paper you measure a pH of about 2 to 3.
89235.m: With a pH of about 2 to 3, lemon juice is clearly acidic.

89236.q: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strongly acidic solution?
89236.e: The more acidic a solution is, the redder the colour. Strongly acidic solutions with pH 1 or 2 turn it red.
89236.m: Strongly acidic solutions turn universal indicator red.

89237.q: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strongly alkaline solution?
89237.e: As the pH rises, the colour changes through blue to violet. That is why strong alkalis turn it dark blue to violet.
89237.m: Strong alkalis turn universal indicator blue to violet.

89238.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution at room temperature?
89238.e: The pH scale usually goes from 0 to 14. Pure water is neutral and has a pH of 7 at room temperature.
89238.m: Neutral solutions have a pH of 7.

89239.q: A solution has a pH of 3. What is it like?
89239.e: All values below 7 mean acidic. A pH of 3 shows a clearly acidic solution.

89240.q: Solution A has pH 2, solution B has pH 5. Which statement is true?
a: Solution A is more acidic than solution B
Solution B is more acidic than solution A
89240.e: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution. With each pH step, the concentration of acid particles changes tenfold.
89240.m: The lower the pH, the more acidic a solution is.

89241.q: How do you measure the pH with universal indicator paper?
a: You compare the colour of the paper with a colour chart
You measure how quickly the paper dries
You hold the paper up to the light and count the dots
89241.e: You dip the paper briefly into the solution. Then you compare the colour with the colour chart on the packet.
89241.m: You read the pH from indicator paper by comparing it with a colour chart.

89242.q: Roughly what colour does universal indicator turn in soapy water with pH 9 to 10?
89242.e: Soapy water is slightly alkaline. At these pH values, universal indicator turns blue.
89242.m: Slightly alkaline solutions such as soapy water turn universal indicator blue.

89243.q: What forms when an acid is neutralised with an alkali?
89243.e: The hydrogen ions of the acid and the hydroxide ions of the alkali join to form water. The other ions form a salt.
89243.m: An acid and an alkali react to form salt and water.

89244.q: Which salt forms when hydrochloric acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide solution?
89244.e: HCl and NaOH make NaCl and H2O. Sodium chloride is our table salt.
89244.m: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution give table salt and water.

89246.q: What do you feel on the beaker when you mix hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
89246.e: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction. Heat is given off to the surroundings.

89247.q: What is the method called where you add an alkali drop by drop to an acid until the indicator changes colour?
89247.e: In a titration you add a solution of known concentration drop by drop. The colour change of the indicator shows the neutral point.
89247.m: A titration tells you how much acid or alkali a solution contains.

89248.q: Why do farmers sometimes spread lime on their fields?
a: To neutralise soil that is too acidic
89248.e: Lime is basic and neutralises acids in the soil. Many plants grow better in soil that is not too acidic.

89249.q: You mix equal amounts of acid particles and alkali particles. Roughly what is the pH of the solution afterwards?
89249.e: When acid and alkali cancel each other out exactly, the solution is neutral. With hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution, the pH is then 7.
89249.m: When acid and alkali cancel each other out exactly, the solution is neutral.

89250.q: Which home remedy can you take for mild heartburn because it neutralises stomach acid?
89250.e: Bicarbonate of soda is weakly basic and neutralises excess stomach acid. Carbon dioxide forms, which is why you often have to burp.
89250.m: Bicarbonate of soda neutralises excess stomach acid.

89251.q: Why does limescale form mainly where water is heated?
a: When heated, the lime dissolved in the water comes out as a solid coating
The lime comes from the metal of the appliance
When heated, dust from the air falls into the water
89251.e: Tap water contains dissolved calcium and hydrogen carbonate ions. When it is heated, carbon dioxide escapes and the lime settles as a white coating.
89251.m: When hard water is heated, limescale is deposited.

89252.q: Which substance is a typical active ingredient in descalers?
a: An acid such as citric acid
An alkali such as sodium hydroxide solution
89252.e: Descalers contain acids such as citric acid or sulphamic acid. Acids dissolve limescale.
89252.m: Descalers contain acids because acids dissolve limescale.

89253.q: Why do you rinse a coffee machine several times with clean water after descaling it?
a: So no descaler ends up in the coffee
89253.e: Leftover acidic descaler would make the coffee taste sour. That is why you run clean water through it several times afterwards.
89253.m: After descaling, rinse thoroughly with clean water.

89254.q: Why does more limescale form in appliances in some regions of Switzerland than in others?
a: Because the tap water there is harder
Because the air there is damper
Because the appliances there are older
89254.e: Water that flows through limestone takes up many calcium and magnesium ions and is hard. Hard water leaves more limescale.
89254.m: Hard water leaves more limescale than soft water.

89255.q: What does it mean when tap water is ‘hard’?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
89255.e: Hard water contains many dissolved calcium and magnesium particles. When it is heated, these form limescale.
89255.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

89256.q: Which kitchen ingredient can you use for descaling?
89256.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. This dissolves limescale, for example on shower heads or taps.
89256.m: Vinegar descales because it contains acetic acid.

89257.q: Why should you descale a coffee machine regularly?
a: Limescale blocks the pipes and makes heating less efficient
89257.e: Limescale builds up on heating elements and in thin pipes. The appliance then needs more energy and can get blocked.
89257.m: Limescale blocks appliances and wastes energy.

89258.q: Why should you not mix descaler with cleaners containing chlorine?
89258.e: Acids release poisonous chlorine gas from cleaners containing chlorine. That is why such products must never be used together.
89258.m: Never mix acidic cleaners with chlorine cleaners.

89259.q: Which organ does the acidic food mixture go to directly after the stomach?
89259.e: After the stomach comes the small intestine. There the acid is neutralised and the food is digested further.
89259.m: After the stomach, the food mixture goes into the small intestine.

89260.q: Which pH is typical for stomach juice when the stomach is empty?
89260.e: In an empty stomach, the stomach juice is strongly acidic. After eating, the pH rises a little because the food buffers the acid.
89260.m: Stomach juice is strongly acidic in an empty stomach.

89261.q: What is one of the jobs of stomach acid?
a: It kills many germs in food
89261.e: The strongly acidic conditions in the stomach kill many bacteria that enter the body with food. It also helps with digestion.
89261.m: Stomach acid protects against many germs from food.

89262.q: Which nutrient is partly digested in the stomach with the help of acid and the enzyme pepsin?
89262.e: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin. Pepsin splits proteins into smaller pieces.
89262.m: The digestion of proteins begins in the stomach.

89263.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall
The stomach wall is made of metal
The acid is neutral in the stomach
The stomach completely renews itself every second
89263.e: The stomach lining makes a thick mucus that covers the wall. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
89263.m: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

a: Stomach acid gets into the gullet
Too much water in the gut
89264.e: When acidic stomach contents flow back into the gullet, they irritate its lining. You feel a burning behind the breastbone.
89264.m: With heartburn, stomach acid rises into the gullet.

89265.q: What kind of substance helps against too much stomach acid?
89265.e: Basic substances neutralise acids. That is why remedies for heartburn contain basic compounds.

89266.q: Where in the body is the acidic stomach juice made?
89266.e: Special cells in the stomach lining, the parietal cells, release hydrochloric acid. Other cells make mucus and enzymes.
89266.m: Stomach acid is made by cells in the stomach lining.

89267.q: Below roughly what pH do we speak of acid rain?
89267.e: Even clean rain is slightly acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; its pH is about 5.6. If it is lower, we speak of acid rain.
89267.m: Rain with a pH below about 5.6 counts as acid rain.

89268.q: Which gas from burning coal and heating oil contributes especially to acid rain?
89268.e: Coal and heating oil contain sulphur. Burning them produces sulphur dioxide, which turns into sulphuric acid in the air.
89268.m: Sulphur dioxide from coal and oil causes acid rain.

89269.q: Which gases from car engines also contribute to acid rain?
89269.e: In hot engines, nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides. In the air these form nitric acid.
89269.m: Nitrogen oxides from engines form nitric acid in the air.

89270.q: Which damage caused by acid rain did people in Switzerland debate especially hotly in the 1980s?
89270.e: In the 1980s, people argued intensely about damage to trees under the slogan ‘forest dieback’. Acid rain counted as an important cause.
89270.m: Acid rain started the debate about forest dieback in the 1980s.

89271.q: Why are marble statues worn away especially badly by acid rain?
a: Marble is made of lime, which is dissolved by acids
Marble dissolves in water like sugar
89271.e: Like limestone, marble is made of calcium carbonate. Acids slowly dissolve it, so statues lose their details.
89271.m: Acid rain eats away buildings made of limestone and marble.

89272.q: Which measure greatly reduced acid rain in Europe?
a: Filters that remove sulphur from exhaust gases
89272.e: Flue gas desulphurisation in power stations and low-sulphur fuels greatly cut the release of sulphur dioxide. Since then rain has been much less acidic.
89272.m: Removing sulphur from exhaust gases has greatly reduced acid rain.

89274.q: What can happen to fish in lakes that have become very acidic from acid rain?
a: They can die because the water is too acidic
89274.e: Many kinds of fish can only cope with slightly acidic water. In very acidic lakes in Scandinavia, whole fish populations died for this reason.

89275.q: How can you tell that an acid is reacting with limestone?
a: It fizzes and forms gas bubbles
The stone gets hot and glows
89275.e: The reaction produces a gas. The bubbles make the acid fizz on the stone.
89275.m: Limestone fizzes when it comes into contact with acid.

89276.q: How do geologists test in the field whether a rock contains lime?
a: They drip dilute hydrochloric acid on it
They put it in salt water
They hold a magnet to it
89276.e: If the rock fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, it contains calcium carbonate. This is called the acid test.
89276.m: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used to test rock for lime.

89277.q: What is the chemical formula of calcium carbonate, the main part of limestone?
89277.e: Calcium carbonate is made of calcium ions and carbonate ions (CO3). This gives the formula CaCO3.
89277.m: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3.

89278.q: What happens to the shell of a raw egg if you leave the egg in vinegar for a day?
89278.e: Eggshells are mainly calcium carbonate. The acetic acid dissolves the shell, and only the soft skin is left.
89278.m: Vinegar dissolves eggshells, which contain lime.

89279.q: Which rock forms when limestone is changed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure?
89279.e: Under great heat and high pressure, limestone is changed into marble. That is why marble, like limestone, is made of calcium carbonate.

a: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves the limestone
Volcanoes blast holes in the rock
89280.e: Rainwater takes in carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic. Over a long time it dissolves the lime and forms hollow spaces.
89280.m: Slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and so forms caves.

89281.q: Which of these substances is also mainly made of calcium carbonate?
89281.e: Chalk, limestone and marble are all mainly made of calcium carbonate. Granite and quartz, on the other hand, are mainly made of silicates.
89281.m: Like limestone, chalk is made of calcium carbonate.

89282.q: Which household product removes limescale from a kettle?
89282.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. The acid dissolves the limescale, and bubbles of carbon dioxide form.
89282.m: Acids such as vinegar dissolve limescale.

89283.q: Which fruits contain especially large amounts of citric acid?
89283.e: Citrus fruits such as lemons and limes contain a lot of citric acid. It gives them their sour taste.
89283.m: Lemons and limes are rich in citric acid.

89284.q: What is citric acid often used for in the home?
89284.e: Citric acid dissolves limescale. That is why it is used to descale kettles and coffee machines.

89285.q: What does pure citric acid look like at room temperature?
89285.e: Pure citric acid is a colourless to white solid. You buy it as a powder, for example for descaling.
89285.m: Pure citric acid is a white powder.

89286.q: With which living thing is most citric acid made industrially today?
89286.e: Today citric acid is mainly made from sugar using the mould Aspergillus niger. Lemons alone could not meet the demand.
89286.m: Citric acid is made industrially with moulds.

89287.q: What are the salts of citric acid called?
89287.e: The salts and esters of citric acid are called citrates. One example is sodium citrate, which is found in foods.
89287.m: The salts of citric acid are called citrates.

89288.q: What is the citric acid cycle in our cells for?
89288.e: In the citric acid cycle, cells get energy from nutrients. Citric acid is an important substance along the way.
89288.m: The citric acid cycle supplies cells with energy.

89289.q: Why can citric acid remove limescale from a kettle?
a: The acid makes the limescale magnetic
The acid makes the limescale invisible
89289.e: Acids react with limescale. The limescale dissolves and can be rinsed away.
89289.m: Acids such as citric acid dissolve limescale.

89290.q: Where did citric acid come from in the past, before people made it with moulds?
89290.e: In the 18th century, citric acid first came from lemon juice. Today it is mainly made from sugar using moulds.
89290.m: Citric acid was first obtained from lemon juice.

89291.q: Where is ammonia often used as a refrigerant?
a: In artificial ice rinks and large cold stores
89291.e: In large cooling systems such as artificial ice rinks, ammonia is a proven refrigerant. Because it is poisonous, it is hardly used in small household appliances.
89291.m: Large cooling systems such as ice rinks are often cooled with ammonia.

89292.q: What does ammonia gas smell like?
89292.e: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a very sharp smell. You may know the smell from badly aired stables.
89292.m: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell.

89293.q: What is a solution of ammonia in water like?
a: Different depending on the time of day
89293.e: In water, ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion. This produces hydroxide ions and the solution becomes alkaline.
89293.m: Ammonia forms an alkaline solution with water.

89294.q: What is the well-known process for making ammonia on a large scale called?
89294.e: At the beginning of the 20th century, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
89294.m: Ammonia is made by the Haber-Bosch process.

89295.q: What is most of the ammonia produced used for?
89295.e: Nitrogen fertiliser is made from ammonia. Without this fertiliser, far fewer people in the world could be fed.
89295.m: Ammonia is the raw material for nitrogen fertiliser.

89296.q: What was the old name for a solution of ammonia in water, often used in the past as a cleaning agent?
89296.e: Spirit of hartshorn is ammonia dissolved in water. Ammonia solution is used, for example, in glass cleaners.
89296.m: Spirit of hartshorn is a solution of ammonia in water.

89297.q: Which ion forms when ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion?
89297.e: Ammonia (NH3) takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes the ammonium ion (NH4+). Ammonium salts are found in many fertilisers.
89297.m: Ammonia and a hydrogen ion make the ammonium ion.

89298.q: Is ammonia gas lighter or heavier than air?
89298.e: Ammonia has a lower density than air. That is why escaping ammonia rises upwards.
89298.m: Ammonia gas is lighter than air.

89496.q: Which data does the Swiss Data Protection Act protect?
89496.e: The Data Protection Act sets out how information relating to a specific or identifiable person is handled. This includes things like name, address or photos.
89496.m: The Data Protection Act protects information about people.

89497.q: Under the Swiss Data Protection Act, what must a company do if it collects data about you?
a: Report the data to your school
89497.e: Companies have a duty to inform. They must say which data they collect and what they use it for.
89497.m: Anyone who collects personal data must inform the people concerned.

89498.q: What is the job of the FDPIC in Switzerland?
89498.e: FDPIC stands for Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner. It checks whether authorities and companies comply with the Data Protection Act and advises the public.
