89901.e: A sound usually reaches one ear a little earlier and louder. That way the brain notices which direction it comes from.
89901.m: With two ears you can hear the direction of a sound.

89902.q: What should you not push deep into your ear?
89902.e: Cotton buds can push earwax deeper or injure the eardrum. You only clean the outer ear.
89902.m: Cotton buds do not belong deep in the ear.

89903.e: Earwax traps dust and dirt. It protects the ear canal and moves outwards by itself.

89904.q: What vibrates on a drum when you hit it?
a: The air in the next room
89904.e: The tight skin of the drum vibrates after the hit. We hear this vibration as a sound.
89904.m: On a drum, the skin vibrates.

89905.e: A big skin vibrates more slowly than a small one. Slow vibrations sound low.

89906.q: What do you usually hit a drum with?
89906.e: Drums are played with drumsticks, beaters or the hands. This makes the skin start to vibrate.
89906.m: Drums are played with sticks or beaters.

89907.q: What drumming music is the city of Basel famous for?
89907.e: At the Basel carnival, many drummers and pipers march through the city. Since 2017, the Basel carnival has been part of UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage.
89907.m: Basel is famous for drumming at the carnival.

89908.q: What is a person who plays the drum in a Swiss band often also called?
89908.e: In Switzerland, drummers are often called tambours. The word comes from French.
89908.m: In Switzerland, a drummer is often called a tambour.

89909.q: What is the large kettledrum in the orchestra called?
89909.e: The timpani have a large kettle-shaped body with a skin over it. They can be tuned to different notes.

89910.q: What happens to the sound when you tighten the drumskin?
89910.e: A tight skin vibrates faster. Fast vibrations sound higher.

89911.q: How can you see that a drumskin is vibrating?
a: Grains of rice jump on it
It gets as warm as an oven
89911.e: If you put a few grains of rice on the skin and hit next to them, they jump. That way you can see the vibration.
89911.m: Jumping rice grains show the skin vibrating.

89912.q: What do you need a tuning fork for?
89912.e: A tuning fork always gives exactly the same note. Musicians tune their instruments to it.
89912.m: You tune instruments with a tuning fork.

89913.q: How many prongs does a tuning fork have?
89913.e: A tuning fork has two prongs, like a U with a handle. The two prongs vibrate towards and away from each other.
89913.m: A tuning fork has two prongs.

89914.q: Which note does a standard tuning fork give?
89914.e: Most tuning forks give concert pitch A. It vibrates 440 times per second.
89914.m: A tuning fork usually gives concert pitch A.

89915.q: What happens if you hold a sounding tuning fork in water?
89915.e: The prongs vibrate back and forth very fast. In water you can see this, because it splashes.
89915.m: A sounding tuning fork makes water splash.

89916.q: How do you make a tuning fork sound?
a: You put it in the light
89916.e: You tap the prongs lightly against something soft, for example your knee. Then they start to vibrate.
89916.m: A tuning fork sounds when you tap it.

89917.q: What happens to the sound if you stand a sounding tuning fork on a table by its handle?
89917.e: The table vibrates too and passes the sound on to much more air. That is why the note sounds louder.
89917.m: A table makes the tuning fork's note louder.

89918.q: How do you stop the sound of a tuning fork?
89918.e: With your fingers you stop the vibrating prongs. Without vibration there is no more sound.
89918.m: Touching the prongs stops the sound.

89919.q: Where do you hold a tuning fork when you tap it?
a: You do not, it lies down
89919.e: You hold the tuning fork by the handle. That way the prongs can vibrate freely.
89919.m: Hold a tuning fork by the handle.

89920.q: What do you need for a tin can telephone?
a: A mobile phone and a tin
89920.e: A tin can telephone is made of two tins or cups joined by a long string. You do not need a cable.
89920.m: A tin can telephone needs two tins and a string.

89921.q: How must the string of a tin can telephone be?
89921.e: Only a tight string passes the vibrations on well. A loose string damps them.
89921.m: On a tin can telephone, the string must be tight.

89922.q: What does the sound travel through to the other cup on a tin can telephone?
89922.e: The vibrations of the voice travel along the tight string to the other cup.
89922.m: On a tin can telephone, the sound travels through the string.

89923.q: What vibrates on a tin can telephone when you speak into it?
89923.e: Your voice makes the bottom of the tin vibrate. At the other end, the bottom of the second tin vibrates too.
89923.m: On a tin can telephone, the bottom of the tin vibrates.

89924.q: What happens if someone holds the string of the tin can telephone in the middle?
89924.e: The hand stops the vibrations of the string. Then hardly any sound reaches the other end.
89924.m: Holding the string stops the sound.

89925.q: What can you use instead of tins for a string telephone?
89925.e: Yoghurt pots have a firm bottom that vibrates well. Soft things such as cotton wool or fabric swallow the sound.
89925.m: You can build a string telephone with yoghurt pots too.

89926.q: What do you do with the second tin when the other person is speaking?
a: You hold it to your ear
You put it in the fridge
89926.e: With a tin can telephone, one person speaks into the tin and the other holds their tin to their ear. Then you swap.
89926.m: When listening, you hold the tin to your ear.

89927.q: Does a tin can telephone need electricity?
89927.e: The tin can telephone works only with vibrations. It needs no electricity.
89927.m: A tin can telephone works without electricity.

89928.q: What does not vibrate when you whisper, unlike when you speak normally?
89928.e: When you speak normally, the vocal folds in the larynx vibrate. When you whisper, they stay still and you only hear the sound of air.
89928.m: When whispering, the vocal folds do not vibrate.

89929.q: What is the game called where a word is passed on in a whisper?
89929.e: In “Telephone”, everyone whispers the word into their neighbour's ear. At the end, something quite different often comes out.
89929.m: In Telephone, you pass a word on in a whisper.

89930.e: When someone is asleep, you do not want to wake them. That is why you whisper.
89930.m: You whisper so others are not disturbed.

89931.q: How loud is whispering compared with normal speaking?
89931.e: When you whisper, only air without voice comes out of your mouth. That is why it is much quieter than normal speaking.

89932.q: What do you often hold round your mouth when whispering so only one person hears?
89932.e: A hand round your mouth directs the sound straight into the other person's ear. So the others hear less.
89932.m: With a hand at your mouth, you whisper more precisely.

89933.q: Which sounds can you hear well when someone whispers?
89933.e: Hissing sounds like “s” and “sh” are made with air alone. That is why you can hear them well even in a whisper.
89933.m: You can hear hissing sounds well even in a whisper.

89934.q: What is a teacher usually doing when they say “Shh”?
89934.e: “Shh” is a quiet hissing sound. It means: please be quiet.

89935.q: Can you hear a whisper well from a long way away?
a: Yes, as far as the next village
89935.e: Whispering is very quiet and gets weaker quickly with distance. That is why you only hear it from close by.
89935.m: You only hear whispering from close by.

89936.q: Why do people wear ear protection?
a: To protect the ears from noise
89936.e: Ear protection makes loud noises quieter. That way your hearing is not damaged.
89936.m: Ear protection protects the ears from noise.

89937.q: Which ear protection do you put straight into your ears?
89937.e: Earplugs are small, soft plugs. You put them into the ear canal.

89938.q: Where do workers often wear ear protection?
89938.e: On a building site, machines such as drills and pneumatic drills are very loud. That is why the workers wear ear protection.
89938.m: On loud building sites, people wear ear protection.

89939.q: When is ear protection a good idea for children?
89939.e: Fireworks, for example on 1 August, can bang very loudly. Ear protection protects sensitive ears.
89939.m: At loud fireworks, ear protection protects the ears.

89940.q: What do ear defenders look like?
89940.e: Ear defenders have two padded cups on a headband. They cover the whole ears.
89940.m: Ear defenders look like big headphones.

89941.q: Do damaged hearing cells in the ear grow back by themselves?
89941.e: The fine hearing cells in the inner ear do not grow back. That is why it is important to protect your hearing.
89941.m: Damaged hearing cells do not grow back.

89942.q: At carnival, a Guggenmusik band is playing very loudly. What protects your ears?
89942.e: Close to loudspeakers or Guggenmusik bands it is very loud. Earplugs make the noise quieter and protect your ears.

89943.q: What is a sign that it was too loud?
89943.e: After very loud noise, your ears sometimes beep or ring. This is a warning sign for your hearing.
89943.m: A ringing in the ears warns of too much noise.

89944.q: In a thunderstorm, what reaches us first?
89944.e: Light is much faster than sound. That is why you see the lightning before you hear the thunder.
89944.m: In a thunderstorm, you see the lightning before the thunder.

89945.q: What makes the loud thunder in a thunderstorm?
a: The lightning heats the air very quickly
Two clouds bump into each other
The wind whistles over the mountains
89945.e: Lightning heats the air extremely strongly in a flash. The air suddenly expands, and that makes the loud bang.
89945.m: Thunder happens because lightning heats the air.

89946.q: About how far away is a thunderstorm if you count 3 seconds between lightning and thunder?
89946.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. So at 3 seconds, the storm is about 1 kilometre away.
89946.m: Three seconds between lightning and thunder is about one kilometre.

89947.q: About how far away is a thunderstorm if you count 9 seconds?
89947.e: You divide the seconds by 3. 9 divided by 3 is 3, so the storm is about 3 kilometres away.
89947.m: Divide the seconds by three to get the kilometres.

89948.q: What does it mean when lightning and thunder come almost at the same time?
89948.e: The shorter the time between lightning and thunder, the closer the storm. Then you should be safely indoors.
89948.m: If lightning and thunder come together, the storm is close.

89949.q: Why does thunder often rumble and roll for a long time?
a: The sound from near and far arrives at different times
The wind blows the thunder further
The rain makes the thunder longer
89949.e: A flash of lightning is very long. The sound from near and far parts arrives at different times, and mountains throw it back.
89949.m: Thunder rolls because its sound travels for different lengths of time.

89950.q: Where is the best place to go when there is thunder?
a: Into a lake for a swim
89950.e: In a thunderstorm, you are safest in a house or a car. Lone trees, summits and water are dangerous.
89950.m: When it thunders, go into a house.

89951.q: In a thunderstorm, what do you really need to take shelter from, the thunder or the lightning?
89951.e: Thunder is only loud; it does not hurt. The lightning is what is dangerous.
89951.m: The lightning is dangerous, not the thunder.

89952.q: About how long should you stay indoors after the last thunder?
89952.e: Even a storm that is moving away can still send lightning. That is why you wait about half an hour after the last thunder.
89952.m: After the last thunder, wait about half an hour.

89953.q: What do you need a megaphone for?
89953.e: A megaphone makes your voice louder. So even people far away can hear what you are saying.
89953.m: A megaphone makes your voice louder.

89954.e: A megaphone is wide at the front and narrow at the back, like a funnel. You speak into the narrow end.
89954.m: A megaphone is shaped like a funnel.

89955.q: In German, a megaphone is jokingly called “Flüstertüte”. What does that mean?
89955.e: As a joke, the megaphone is called a “whisper bag” in German. Yet it actually makes the voice louder.
89955.m: In German, a megaphone is jokingly called a whisper bag.

89956.e: The fire brigade and police use megaphones to tell lots of people outdoors something. Coaches and tour guides use them too.
89956.m: The fire brigade and police often use a megaphone.

89957.q: What do electric megaphones need to work?
89957.e: Electric megaphones have a loudspeaker. It gets its electricity from batteries.

89958.q: How can you make a simple megaphone with your hands?
a: Hold your hands like a funnel round your mouth
Put your hands over your ears
Put your hands in your pockets
89958.e: If you hold your hands like a funnel round your mouth, your call is focused. So it can be heard further away.
89958.m: With your hands round your mouth, your call carries further.

89959.q: What can you use to make a simple megaphone yourself?
89959.e: A piece of card rolled into a funnel focuses the sound. That makes your voice louder.
89959.m: A card funnel is a simple megaphone.

89960.q: In which direction is a megaphone especially loud?
89960.e: The funnel focuses the sound forwards. Behind the megaphone it is quieter.
89960.m: A megaphone is loudest towards the front.

89961.q: What material is an alphorn usually made of?
89961.e: An alphorn is usually made of wood, often spruce. In the past, people used a tree that had grown crooked on a slope.
89961.m: An alphorn is usually made of wood.

89962.q: Which country is the alphorn especially known for?
89962.e: The alphorn is a symbol of Swiss folk music. You hear it at festivals and in the mountains.
89962.m: The alphorn is typical of Switzerland.

89963.q: How many finger holes or keys does an alphorn have?
89963.e: An alphorn has no holes, keys or valves. It is simply a long, open tube with a mouthpiece.
89963.m: An alphorn has no finger holes.

89964.q: What does the alphorn player use to make the different notes?
89964.e: The player blows into the mouthpiece and tightens the lips by different amounts. This makes higher or lower notes.
89964.m: On the alphorn, you make the notes with your lips.

89965.q: What did herders use the alphorn for in the past?
89965.e: The sound of the alphorn can be heard a long way off. Herders used it to give signals across the Alps.
89965.m: In the past, herders gave signals with the alphorn.

89966.q: Why can you hear the alphorn so far away?
a: It has a loud, carrying sound
89966.e: The long tube makes a strong, deep sound. It carries far over valleys and mountains.
89966.m: The alphorn's strong sound carries far.

89967.q: What shape is the end of an alphorn?
89967.e: The lower end of the alphorn is curved upwards and wide open. This shape comes from the tree that grew crooked.
89967.m: The end of the alphorn curves upwards.

90065.q: Roughly what is the average air pressure at sea level?
90065.e: Standard pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals. The actual value varies with the weather.
90065.m: At sea level, the average air pressure is about 1013 hectopascals.

90066.q: In which unit do weather services such as MeteoSwiss usually give air pressure?
90066.e: One hectopascal equals 100 pascals. People used to say millibars instead; the number is the same.
90066.m: Air pressure is given in hectopascals.

90067.q: Near the ground, by roughly how much does air pressure fall for every 8 metres of height?
90067.e: At low altitudes, air pressure falls by about 1 hectopascal for roughly every 8 metres you climb. Higher up, the decrease becomes slower.
90067.m: The higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

90068.q: At what height is air pressure about half as great as at sea level?
90068.e: At about 5.5 kilometres up, only half of the air’s mass is above you. That is why the pressure there is about half as great.
90068.m: At 5500 metres, the air pressure is only half as great.

a: The weight of the air above us
90069.e: Air has weight. The whole column of air above a surface presses down on it and so creates air pressure.
90069.m: The weight of the column of air creates air pressure.

90070.q: When there are pressure differences, in which direction does air basically flow?
90070.e: Air evens out pressure differences, so it flows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. This creates wind.
90070.m: Wind is caused by differences in air pressure.

90071.q: Why does water boil below 100 °C on a high mountain?
a: Because the air pressure there is lower
Because the water there is cleaner
Because the sun shines more strongly there
Because the air there is damper
90071.e: At lower air pressure, water molecules can turn into gas more easily. On the Jungfraujoch, water boils below 90 °C.
90071.m: At low air pressure, water boils sooner.

90072.e: Hecto means 100. So you work out 1013 times 100 and get 101,300 pascals.
90072.m: One hectopascal equals a hundred pascals.

90073.q: How does the air pressure change in a train travelling from Interlaken up to the Jungfraujoch?
90073.e: With every metre of height, there is less air above the train. So the air pressure falls, and you often feel pressure in your ears.
90073.m: Air pressure falls as height increases.

90074.q: How does the air move in the centre of a high-pressure area?
90074.e: In a high, air sinks from high up to the ground and flows outwards there.
90074.m: In a high, the air sinks.

90075.q: Why do clouds usually disappear in a high-pressure area?
a: Sinking air warms up and dries out.
The wind blows all the clouds away.
The sun evaporates the clouds from above.
The clouds fall down as rain.
90075.e: Sinking air is compressed and so gets warmer. Warm air can hold more water vapour, so the cloud droplets evaporate.

90076.q: In the northern hemisphere, in which direction does air flow around a high?
90076.e: Because the Earth rotates, the air flowing out is deflected. In the northern hemisphere this makes it turn clockwise around the high.
90076.m: Here, air circles a high clockwise.

90077.q: Which high over the Atlantic often brings Switzerland fine weather in summer?
90077.e: The Azores High usually lies west of Portugal. When it stretches as far as central Europe in summer, it becomes sunny in Switzerland too.
90077.m: The Azores High often brings summer weather.

90078.q: What weather does a high often bring to the Swiss Central Plateau in winter?
90078.e: In calm high-pressure weather, cold, damp air collects in the Central Plateau. A grey blanket of fog lies over it, while it is sunny in the mountains.
90078.m: A winter high often brings a blanket of low cloud to the Central Plateau.

90079.q: What is the weather situation called in which warmer air lies above colder air in a high?
90079.e: Normally it gets colder as you go up. In an inversion it is the other way round, and the cold air stays trapped near the ground.
90079.m: In an inversion, warm air lies above cold air.

90080.q: Which cold north-easterly wind often blows in the Central Plateau when a high lies north of Switzerland?
90080.e: When a high lies over northern Europe, cold air flows from the north-east between the Jura and the Alps. On Lake Geneva the bise is often especially strong.
90080.m: The bise is a cold wind from the north-east.

90081.q: What is a high-pressure area called in technical language?
90081.e: “Anti” means “against”. An anticyclone is the opposite of a cyclone, which is a low.
90081.m: In technical language, a high is called an anticyclone.

90082.q: How does the air move in the centre of a low-pressure area?
90082.e: In a low, air flows together at the ground and then rises.
90082.m: In a low, the air rises.

90083.q: In the northern hemisphere, in which direction does air flow around a low?
90083.e: The Earth’s rotation deflects the air flowing in. In the northern hemisphere it therefore turns anticlockwise around the low.
90083.m: Here, air circles a low anticlockwise.

90084.q: In summer, what does very cold air high up over warm ground often bring?
90084.e: Warm air from the ground rises into the cold air high up. Tall heaped clouds grow, which produce showers and thunderstorms.
90084.m: Cold air high up over warm ground often brings thunderstorms.

90085.q: From which direction do low-pressure areas usually move towards Switzerland?
a: From the west, from the Atlantic
From the north, from the North Pole
90085.e: In our latitudes, westerly winds mainly blow high up. They drive the lows from the Atlantic across Europe.
90085.m: Lows usually come to us from the Atlantic.

90086.q: What is the common low-pressure area over the North Atlantic called?
90086.e: Around Iceland the air pressure is low on average. Many lows that move towards Europe form or grow stronger there.
90086.m: The Icelandic Low is an important weather maker for Europe.

90087.q: From a weather science point of view, what is a hurricane?
a: A cold front in the Alps
A wind without any pressure difference
90087.e: Hurricanes form over warm tropical seas. In the centre the air pressure is very low.
90087.m: A hurricane is a tropical low-pressure area.

90088.q: Why do many clouds form in a low?
90088.e: When air rises, it expands and cools. The water vapour condenses into cloud droplets.

90089.q: Where in Switzerland does a Genoa low often bring especially a lot of rain or snow?
a: On the south side of the Alps, for example in Ticino
90089.e: A low over the Gulf of Genoa carries damp air from the Mediterranean towards the Alps. On the south side of the Alps it then often rains or snows heavily.
90089.m: A Genoa low often brings Ticino a lot of rain or snow.

a: The boundary between two different air masses
A line of equal wind strength
The edge of a single cloud
The boundary between day and night
90090.e: At a front, air masses with different temperatures and humidity meet. The weather often changes clearly there.
90090.m: A front separates warm and cold air masses.

90091.q: What is it called when a cold front catches up with the warm front ahead of it?
90091.e: The cold front is faster and catches up with the warm front. The warm air is lifted up off the ground.
90091.m: In an occlusion, the cold front catches up with the warm front.

90092.q: Which front often brings short, heavy showers and thunderstorms?
90092.e: The cold air pushes quickly under the warm air and lifts it steeply. This creates tall thunderclouds with heavy showers.
90092.m: Cold fronts often bring showers and thunderstorms.

90093.q: Where does the term “front” in weather science come from?
a: From the battle lines of the First World War
From the front of a house
From the bow of a ship
90093.e: Norwegian researchers compared the meeting of air masses with the front lines of the First World War.
90093.m: Weather fronts are named after military front lines.

90094.q: What is the area between a warm front and the cold front that follows it called?
90094.e: Behind the warm front lies the warm air of the low. This area reaches as far as the next cold front.
90094.m: The warm sector lies between the warm front and the cold front.

90095.q: What do you call a front that hardly moves?
90095.e: At a stationary front, neither air mass pushes the other away. Then it can rain in the same place for a long time.
90095.m: A stationary front stays almost in the same place.

90096.q: In central Europe, which pressure system are warm and cold fronts usually attached to?
90096.e: Fronts form in the swirl of a low. They move across the land together with the low.
90096.m: Weather fronts usually belong to a low-pressure area.

90097.q: What almost always changes when a front passes?
90097.e: Behind a front there is a different air mass. So after it passes, it gets warmer or colder.
90097.m: With a front, the air mass changes and so does the temperature.

90098.q: What happens at a cold front?
a: Cold air pushes under warm air.
Warm air glides over cold air.
Cold air rises over warm air.
90098.e: Cold air is heavier. It pushes like a wedge under the warm air and lifts it quickly.
90098.m: At a cold front, cold air pushes under the warm air.

90099.q: What weather does a cold front often bring in summer?
90099.e: The warm air is lifted quickly and steeply. Tall heaped clouds form, with showers, gusts and thunderstorms.

90100.q: What happens to the air temperature after a cold front has passed?
90100.e: Cooler air follows behind the cold front. In summer, the temperature can drop by ten degrees or more within a short time.
90100.m: After a cold front it gets cooler.

90101.q: What symbol shows a cold front on a weather map?
90101.e: The triangles point in the direction the front is moving. The blue colour stands for the cold air.
90101.m: A cold front is drawn in blue with triangles.

90102.e: The heavy cold air pushes forward strongly. That is why the cold front often catches up with the warm front.
90102.m: Cold fronts are usually faster than warm fronts.

90103.q: Which type of cloud is typical of an active cold front?
90103.e: Cumulonimbus is a huge thundercloud that can grow up to the top of the lower atmosphere.
90103.m: A cold front often brings tall thunderclouds.

90104.q: How does the wind often behave when a cold front passes?
a: It picks up in gusts and changes direction.
90104.e: Strong gusts come with the cold front. The wind also usually turns from south-west to west or north-west.
90104.m: At a cold front, the wind becomes gusty.

90105.q: How does the air pressure change after a cold front has passed?
90105.e: Behind the cold front lies heavier, cold air. So the air pressure rises again.
90105.m: After a cold front, air pressure rises.

90106.q: What happens at a warm front?
a: Warm air glides over cold air.
Cold air pushes under warm air.
Warm air sinks to the ground.
90106.e: The lighter warm air slowly rises over the cold air that is still lying near the ground.
90106.m: At a warm front, warm air glides up over cold air.

90107.q: What weather does a warm front often bring?
90107.e: Because the warm air rises slowly, a wide layer of cloud forms. Steady rain often falls from it for hours.
90107.m: Warm fronts often bring long periods of rain.

90108.q: Which clouds often announce a warm front a day in advance?
90108.e: The surface the warm air glides up is very gentle. So the first high cirrus clouds appear far ahead of the actual front.
90108.m: Feathery clouds are often signs of a coming warm front.

90109.q: From which cloud does the long-lasting rain fall at a warm front?
90109.e: Nimbostratus is a thick, grey layer of cloud without a clear shape. Long-lasting rain or snow falls from it.
90109.m: Nimbostratus is the typical rain cloud of a warm front.

90110.q: What symbol shows a warm front on a weather map?
90110.e: The semicircles point in the direction the front is moving. Red stands for the warm air moving in.
90110.m: A warm front is drawn in red with semicircles.

90111.q: Which light effect around the sun can announce an approaching warm front?
90111.e: Thin veil clouds made of ice crystals bend the sunlight. This creates a bright ring around the sun.
90111.m: A ring around the sun can point to a warm front.

90112.q: How does the air pressure change when a warm front is approaching?
90112.e: Ahead of the warm front, the low is approaching. So the air pressure falls slowly and steadily.
90112.m: Air pressure falls ahead of a warm front.

90113.q: How steep is the boundary between warm and cold air at a warm front?
90113.e: The boundary rises only very slowly, often only about one kilometre over 100 kilometres. That is why the clouds reach far ahead.
90113.m: The boundary at a warm front is very gentle.

90114.q: What does relative humidity tell you?
a: What percentage of the possible amount of water vapour the air contains
How many raindrops fall per hour
How heavy a cubic metre of air is
How much water there is in the ground
90114.e: Relative humidity compares the actual amount of water vapour with the greatest possible amount at that temperature.
90114.m: Relative humidity is given as a percentage.

90115.q: Which air can hold more water vapour?
90115.e: The warmer the air, the more water vapour it can hold. At 30 °C it is a good six times as much as at 0 °C.
90115.m: Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air.

90116.q: Air could hold 20 g of water vapour per cubic metre but contains only 10 g. What is the relative humidity?
90116.e: You work out 10 divided by 20, which gives 0.5, or 50 per cent.
90116.m: Relative humidity is the share of the greatest possible amount.

90117.q: In which unit is absolute humidity often given?
90117.e: Absolute humidity tells you how many grams of water vapour there are in one cubic metre of air.
90117.m: Absolute humidity is measured in grams per cubic metre.

90118.q: What happens when the relative humidity reaches 100 per cent?
90118.e: At 100 per cent the air is saturated. Any more water vapour turns into tiny water droplets, for example as fog or cloud.
90118.m: At 100 per cent humidity, the air is saturated.

90119.q: Which relative humidity is considered comfortable in living rooms?
90119.e: Most people feel comfortable in this range. If it stays damper for a long time, mould can form.
90119.m: Living rooms should be neither too dry nor too damp.

90120.q: Why is the air in heated rooms often dry in winter?
a: Cold outside air holds little water vapour and is warmed up indoors.
The heating sucks water out of the air.
There is no water vapour in winter.
90120.e: Cold air contains only a little water vapour. When it is warmed in the house, it could hold much more, so the relative humidity falls sharply.
90120.m: Warmed winter air is relatively dry.

90121.q: What is the typical relative humidity in fog?
90121.e: Fog is made of tiny water droplets that only form in saturated air.
90121.m: In fog, the air is saturated with water vapour.

90122.q: How does relative humidity change when air cools down without any water being added?
90122.e: Cooler air can hold less water vapour. The same amount of water vapour then makes up a bigger share.
90122.m: When air cools, the relative humidity rises.

a: The temperature at which water vapour starts to condense
The place where it rains the most
The time of day when the dew evaporates
The lowest temperature of a year
90123.e: When air cools to the dew point, it is saturated. Then dew, fog or a cloud forms.
90123.m: At the dew point, water vapour starts to condense.

90124.q: Why is there often dew on the grass after clear, still nights?
a: The ground cools below the dew point.
90124.e: Without clouds, the ground gives off a lot of heat. The air right next to the grass cools below the dew point, and water vapour settles.
90124.m: Dew forms when air cools below the dew point at the cold ground.

90125.q: What forms instead of dew when the dew point is below 0 °C?
90125.e: Below freezing point, water vapour settles directly as ice crystals. This creates frost.
90125.m: Below zero degrees, frost forms instead of dew.

90126.q: What does it mean when the air temperature and the dew point are almost the same?
90126.e: The difference between the temperature and the dew point is called the spread. If it is very small, the air is almost saturated.
90126.m: A small gap to the dew point points to fog.

90127.q: Why do your glasses steam up in winter when you come into a warm room?
a: The cold lenses cool the room air below the dew point.
It is drizzling slightly in the room.
90127.e: The lenses are still cold. The warm, damp room air cools below the dew point on them, and droplets form.
90127.m: Damp air condenses on cold surfaces.

90128.q: Why do drops of water form on the outside of a glass with a cold drink?
a: The air at the glass cools below the dew point.
The drink seeps through the glass.
90128.e: The water comes from the air. At the cold glass the air cools below the dew point, and water vapour condenses.
90128.m: The drops on a cold glass come from the air.

90129.q: Rule of thumb: cloud base in metres equals 125 times (temperature minus dew point). How high is it at 20 °C with a dew point of 12 °C?
90129.e: The difference is 20 minus 12, which is 8 degrees. 125 times 8 makes 1000 metres.
90129.m: The bigger the gap to the dew point, the higher the clouds.

90130.q: What does a high dew point of over 18 °C in summer usually show?
90130.e: A high dew point means there is a lot of water vapour in the air. Sweat evaporates badly, and it feels oppressive.
90130.m: A high dew point makes the air muggy.

90131.q: What is the highest the dew point can be?
a: As high as the air temperature
Twice as high as the air temperature
90131.e: When the air is saturated, the temperature and the dew point are the same. The dew point cannot rise any higher.
90131.m: The dew point is never higher than the air temperature.

90133.q: Which liquid did Torricelli’s classic barometer use?
90133.e: Mercury is very heavy. That is why a tube less than one metre long is enough.

90134.q: In which unit does the weather forecast usually give air pressure?
90134.e: Air pressure is usually given in hectopascals (hPa). At sea level it is about 1013 hPa on average.
90134.m: Air pressure is measured in hectopascals.

90135.q: How does an aneroid barometer without liquid work?
a: Air pressure squeezes an almost airless metal box
A small propeller turns in the wind
90135.e: When air pressure is high, the thin box is squeezed; when it is low, the box expands. A pointer passes on this movement.
90135.m: In an aneroid barometer, air pressure moves a metal box.

90136.q: What does it usually mean when the barometer falls sharply within a few hours?
90136.e: Quickly falling air pressure shows that a low is approaching. Wind, clouds and rain often follow.
90136.m: A falling barometer announces worse weather.

90137.q: Which device used by mountain walkers and pilots works on the same principle as a barometer?
90137.e: Because air pressure falls with height, you can calculate the height from the measured pressure.
90137.m: An altimeter actually measures air pressure.

90138.q: What does a barometer at the top of a mountain show compared with the valley?
90138.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is above you. So air pressure falls as you go up, as Blaise Pascal already showed.

90140.e: A hygrometer shows how damp the air is, usually as relative humidity in per cent.

90141.q: What does a classic hair hygrometer use as its sensor?
90141.e: Usually de-greased human hairs are stretched tight. Their length changes with humidity and moves a pointer.
90141.m: The hair hygrometer uses real hairs as its sensor.

90142.q: How does a hair change in damp air?
90142.e: Hairs absorb moisture and stretch slightly. In dry air they shrink back again.
90142.m: Damp air makes hairs a little longer.

90143.q: What can a hygrometer be used for at home?
a: To check whether the room air is too dry or too damp
90143.e: A hygrometer shows the humidity in the room. If it is too high for a long time, mould can form; if it is too low, skin and the lining of your nose dry out.
90143.m: A hygrometer shows whether the room air is too dry or too damp.

90144.q: What does a hygrometer show when the air in a room is very dry?
90144.e: The hygrometer shows the relative humidity in per cent. The drier the air, the lower the number.
90144.m: Dry air has a low humidity percentage.

90145.q: Why does the wet thermometer of a psychrometer show a lower temperature?
a: The water is always ice cold.
90145.e: As water evaporates, it takes heat from the thermometer. The drier the air, the more evaporates and the lower the reading falls.

90146.q: What does the Greek word “hygros” in the name hygrometer mean?
90146.e: “Hygros” means damp and “metron” means measure. So a hygrometer is a dampness meter.

90147.q: How does a modern electronic hygrometer usually measure humidity?
a: With a sensor whose electrical properties change with dampness
90147.e: A thin layer in the sensor takes up water vapour. This changes, for example, its electrical capacitance, which the device converts into per cent.
90147.m: Electronic hygrometers measure dampness with a sensor.

90148.q: Which measuring device is inside a traditional weather house, where a figure comes out depending on the weather?
90148.e: The figures hang on a twisted string made of gut or hair. It twists depending on the humidity and so pushes one figure out.
90148.m: The weather house reacts to humidity.

90149.q: In which colour is a cold front drawn on weather maps?
90149.e: The cold front appears as a blue line with triangles. Blue stands for the cold air moving in behind it.
90149.m: A cold front is drawn in blue with triangles.

90150.q: Why is air pressure converted to sea level for the surface weather map?
a: So that places at different heights can be compared
So that the numbers get smaller
Because weather stations are only by the sea
Because air pressure could not be measured otherwise
90150.e: A station in the mountains always measures lower pressure than one in the valley. Only after converting can you see the real highs and lows.
90150.m: For weather maps, air pressure is converted to sea level.

90151.q: What does the number next to the symbol of a high or low on a weather map tell you?
a: The air pressure in the centre
The wind strength in the centre
The amount of rain in the centre
90151.e: Next to the H or L is the central pressure in hectopascals, for example 1035 for a strong high or 975 for a deep low.
90151.m: The number at a high or low gives the central pressure.

90152.q: On a weather map, what does an arrow with little lines, called a wind barb, show?
90152.e: The arrow shows where the wind is blowing from. The lines at its end give the wind strength.
90152.m: The wind barb shows the direction and strength of the wind.

90153.q: Which invention made the first up-to-date weather maps possible in the 19th century?
90153.e: With the telegraph, measurements from many places could be sent quickly to one place and drawn on a map on the same day.
90153.m: The telegraph made quick weather maps possible.

90154.q: Which letter marks a low on English-language weather maps?
90154.e: In English, a low is called “Low” and a high “High”. That is why the maps show L and H. German maps use T for “Tief”.
90154.m: English weather maps show lows with an L.

90155.q: In what parts is cloud cover given on weather maps?
90155.e: Meteorology divides the sky into eight parts, called oktas. 0 oktas is cloudless, 8 oktas is completely overcast.
90155.m: Cloud cover is given in eighths.

90156.q: What does a weather map in the weather forecast show?
a: The weather over a large area at the same time
The weather in one single place
The weather in a hundred years
90156.e: For a weather map, measurements from many places taken at the same time are brought together. This lets you see highs, lows and fronts.
90156.m: A weather map shows the weather of many places at the same time.

90157.q: What does an isobar on a weather map connect?
a: Places with the same air pressure
Places with the same amount of rain
90157.e: Isobars are lines along which the air pressure is the same everywhere. They show where the highs and lows are.
90157.m: Isobars connect places with the same air pressure.

90158.q: What does it mean when the isobars on a weather map are very close together?
90158.e: Isobars close together show a big pressure difference over a short distance. The air then flows quickly, and it gets stormy.

90159.q: What does the Greek word “isos” in the term isobar mean?
90159.e: “Isos” means equal and “baros” means weight. So an isobar is a line of equal weight, meaning equal pressure.
90159.m: Isobar means line of equal pressure.

90160.q: What do the isobars around a high look like on a weather map?
a: Closed rings with values rising towards the inside
Straight lines from north to south
90160.e: Around a high, the isobars form closed curves. The highest pressure value is in the middle.
90160.m: Isobars lie like rings around a high.

90161.q: How do the numbers on the isobars change as you get closer to the centre of a low?
90161.e: In the centre of a low, the air pressure is lowest. So the values of the isobars decrease towards the inside.
90161.m: Towards the centre of a low, isobar values fall.

90162.q: High up, how does the wind blow compared with the isobars?
90162.e: The Earth’s rotation deflects the air so that high up it flows almost along the isobars. Near the ground, friction slows it, and the wind blows at an angle into the low.
90162.m: High up, the wind blows almost along the isobars.

90163.q: On a weather map, isobars are drawn at intervals of 5 hPa. What is the pressure difference between the first and the fifth isobar?
90163.e: Between the first and the fifth isobar there are 4 gaps. 4 times 5 makes 20 hectopascals.
90163.m: The spacing of isobars shows fixed steps of pressure.

90164.q: Isobars show equal air pressure. What are the matching lines of equal temperature called?
90164.e: “Therm” stands for heat. Isotherms connect places with the same temperature.
90164.m: Lines of equal temperature are called isotherms.

90165.q: What does an exothermic reaction give off to its surroundings?
90165.e: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released, usually as heat. This makes the surroundings warmer.
90165.m: An exothermic reaction gives off heat to its surroundings.

90166.q: Which process is an exothermic reaction?
90166.e: Burning wood releases large amounts of heat and light. The surroundings get noticeably warmer.
90166.m: Every combustion is an exothermic reaction.

90167.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘exo’ in the word exothermic mean?
90167.e: ‘Exo’ means ‘outside’ or ‘out’ and ‘thermos’ means ‘warm’. So exothermic means that heat is given out.
90167.m: Exothermic means that heat goes out.

90168.q: Where are the products of an exothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
a: Not in the diagram at all
90168.e: The products contain less energy than the starting materials. The difference is given off to the surroundings.
90168.m: In exothermic reactions the products have less energy than the starting materials.

90170.q: Disposable hand warmers contain iron powder. Which reaction provides the heat?
90170.e: When you open the packet, the fine iron reacts with oxygen in the air. This rusting happens very fast and gives off heat.
90170.m: The rusting of iron is also an exothermic reaction.

90171.q: What do you notice when you mix dilute hydrochloric acid with dilute sodium hydroxide solution?
a: Nothing, the temperature stays the same
90171.e: The acid and the alkali neutralise each other. This neutralisation is exothermic and warms the solution.
90171.m: Neutralising an acid with an alkali releases heat.

90172.q: What is the highly exothermic thermite reaction of aluminium and iron oxide used for?
90172.e: The thermite reaction produces liquid iron at over 2000 °C. This can be used to join pieces of rail directly on the track.
90172.m: The hot iron from the thermite reaction is used to weld rails together.

90173.q: Why does a candle flame feel hot?
a: The wax takes in heat from the air
The air is compressed by light
90173.e: The wax reacts with oxygen. This releases energy as heat and light.
90173.m: A burning candle gives off energy as heat and light.

90174.q: What does an endothermic reaction do with energy?
90174.e: An endothermic reaction needs energy from its surroundings, for example heat or light. Without a supply of energy it does not continue.
90174.m: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from its surroundings.

90175.q: Where do plants get the energy for endothermic photosynthesis?
90175.e: Plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. The energy is stored in the sugar.
90175.m: Photosynthesis needs the energy of sunlight.

90176.q: Instant cold packs get cold after you snap them. What happens inside?
a: A salt dissolves and takes in heat
A gas burns in the bag
90176.e: Inside the bag a salt such as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. This process takes in heat from the surroundings, so the pack gets cold.
90176.m: A process that takes in heat cools its surroundings.

90178.q: Where are the products of an endothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
90178.e: The products have stored the energy that was taken in. That is why they are higher than the starting materials.
90178.m: In endothermic reactions the products have more energy than the starting materials.

90179.q: Why must the kiln be heated strongly the whole time when making quicklime?
a: Lime gives off a lot of heat
90179.e: Limestone only breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide at around 900 °C. The reaction keeps taking in heat and stops without heating.
90179.m: Making quicklime needs a constant supply of heat.

90180.q: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. What happens if you switch the electricity off?
90180.e: The electrolysis of water is endothermic. It needs a constant supply of electrical energy and stops at once without electricity.
90180.m: Endothermic reactions only run with a constant supply of energy.

90181.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘endo’ in the word endothermic mean?
90181.e: ‘Endo’ means ‘inside’ or ‘in’. In an endothermic reaction, heat goes into the system.
90181.m: Endothermic means that heat goes in.

90182.q: What is meant by activation energy?
a: The energy a reaction needs to start
The energy released at the end
90182.e: For particles to react, bonds must first be loosened. The starting energy needed for this is called activation energy.
90182.m: Activation energy gets a reaction going.

90183.q: Where does the activation energy come from when you strike a match?
a: From the moisture in the air
From the light in the room
From the weight of the match
90183.e: Rubbing the match on the striking surface creates heat. This heat starts the reaction in the match head.
90183.m: The heat of friction can start a reaction.

90184.q: Why does a piece of wood on the table not burn by itself, even though oxygen is there?
90184.e: Burning wood does release energy, but it must be started first. At room temperature there is not enough energy for this.
90184.m: Without starting energy, even burning does not begin.

90185.q: How is activation energy shown in an energy diagram?
a: As an energy hill before the products
As a valley below the starting materials
As an arrow pointing down at the end
90185.e: From the starting materials the curve first rises before it leads to the products. The height of this hill is the activation energy.
90185.m: The activation energy is the energy hill a reaction must get over.

90186.q: What provides the activation energy for combustion in a petrol engine?
a: The spark from the spark plug
90186.e: The spark plug makes an electric spark. It ignites the mixture of petrol vapour and air in the cylinder.
90186.m: In a petrol engine, a spark starts the combustion.

90187.q: Why do many reactions happen faster at higher temperatures?
a: More particles have enough energy to start
90187.e: The warmer it is, the faster the particles move. So more collisions reach the necessary activation energy.
90187.m: Heat helps to reach the activation energy.

90188.q: When does a collision between two particles lead to a reaction?
a: When the particles are the same size
When the particles are standing still
90188.e: Only collisions with at least the activation energy are successful. Weaker collisions make the particles bounce apart unchanged.
90188.m: Only collisions with enough energy lead to a reaction.

90189.q: What does a catalyst do to the energy hill of a reaction?
90189.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy. This makes the reaction start more easily and run faster.
90189.m: A catalyst lowers the energy hill.

90190.q: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?
a: It speeds it up without being used up
It increases the mass of the products
90190.e: A catalyst makes a reaction run faster. At the end it is still there, unchanged.
90190.m: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up itself.

90191.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
90191.e: The catalyst makes a different reaction path possible, with a smaller energy hill. So more particles react in the same time.
90191.m: A catalyst makes the energy hill smaller.

90192.q: Which poisonous gas does a car's catalytic converter turn into carbon dioxide?
90192.e: Carbon monoxide is very poisonous. In the catalytic converter it reacts with oxygen to form less dangerous carbon dioxide.
90192.m: The catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

90193.q: Which precious metal works in many catalytic converters?
90193.e: Catalytic converters contain thin layers of platinum, palladium or rhodium. These metals speed up the conversion of the exhaust gases.
90193.m: Platinum is an important metal in the catalytic converter.

90194.q: What are the catalysts in living things called?
90194.e: Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions in the body. Without them, digestion, for example, would be far too slow.
90194.m: Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

90195.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet after you chew it for a long time?
a: An enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar
The bread gets warm in the mouth
90195.e: Saliva contains an enzyme that splits starch into smaller sugar particles. That is why bread tastes sweetish after long chewing.
90195.m: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch down into sugar.

90196.q: Why does industry use catalysts in many manufacturing processes?
a: The reactions run faster and need less energy
The catalyst becomes the finished product
90196.e: Catalysts speed up reactions, often at lower temperatures too. This saves time, energy and money.
90196.m: Catalysts save time and energy in industry.

90197.q: If you add manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide, it foams a lot. Which gas forms?
90197.e: Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst and speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. This produces water and oxygen.
90197.m: Manganese dioxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

90198.q: Where is the catalytic converter in a car?
90198.e: The catalytic converter is built into the exhaust pipe. The exhaust gases flow through it and are turned into less harmful substances.
90198.m: The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust gases in the exhaust.

90199.q: Why does food go off more slowly in the fridge?
a: There is no air at all in the fridge
The light in the fridge kills germs
90199.e: At low temperatures the particles move more slowly. So breakdown and decay happen more slowly.
